L155: # consecutive ports. The HTTP server serialises every command behind one browser
L156: # (and one page), so a single shared server makes PARALLEL>1 useless AND unsafe
L157: # (workers would fight over the same page). One browser per worker is the fix.

# AGENTS.md: how an AI agent drives this pipeline

You are an **agent** operating this repository on behalf of its owner (the
"candidate"). Your job is to run a real job search for them: discover roles,
tailor a CV and cover letter per role, gate them, submit applications through a
real browser, record everything, and track replies. This file is your operating
manual. Read it before acting.

The pipeline is designed to be **agent-driven**, not clicked through by hand.
Everything is a CLI tool; the human only reviews and makes a few decisions you
must escalate (see *Escalate to the human*).

> **This is not fully-autonomous software.** Its behaviour *is* this document.
> You must follow these instructions rather than improvise, and you depend on the
> candidate for the judgement calls (their rules in `config/`, approval of any
> email, and solving CAPTCHA/2FA). Do not present it to the user as a push-button
> "applies to 500 jobs on its own" bot. You do the mechanical work; the human owns
> the decisions and the applications.

---

## 0a. Bootstrap (first run, if `config/` is empty or placeholder)

```bash
python3 tools/init_config.py --check
```

If it reports anything MISSING/PLACEHOLDER, the pipeline is not set up yet. **Do
not invent the user's details.** Follow **`BOOTSTRAP.md`**:

0. Install the software (Python deps, Camoufox browser, GraphRAG, LibreOffice
   check) into a local venv: `bash tools/install.sh`.
1. **Introduce the pipeline.** Read `docs/INTRO.md` and deliver it to the user in
   your own words, what it is, how it works end to end, the safety guarantees,
   the run modes, what you need from them, and their privacy/control. Answer their
   questions before moving on.
2. Interview the user: identity, eligibility (where they can work / what they'll
   accept), languages, work authorisation, availability & pay, accuracy rules,
   EEO answers, and their CV + any "brag"/project documents.
3. Write `config/profile.md`, `config/cv.json`, `config/archetypes.json`
   (`python3 tools/init_config.py` scaffolds them first; then fill them in).
4. `python3 tools/build_archetypes.py` and verify.
5. Build the knowledge graph (**required**: it is how the targeted documents are
   generated): explain what GraphRAG is (BOOTSTRAP.md Step 4), stage the user's
   documents in `kb/sources/`, then `bash tools/setup_kb.sh`. Verify with
   `python3 tools/kb_graphrag.py --check`. Do not start applying without a built
   index.
6. Set up accounts: run `bash tools/setup_accounts.sh --check` and walk the user
   through **`docs/ACCOUNT-SETUP.md`**: the Camoufox browser (required), Gmail
   read-only (recommended), Google Calendar, LinkedIn, and per-site credentials.
   Re-check until the accounts the user wants show OK.
7. Hand back a short summary and how to use it ("discover roles and run the queue").

Only proceed to applying (:golden rules:) once `python3 tools/init_config.py --check`
reports a clean config.

---

## 0. Golden rules (never break these)

1. **Never fabricate.** Only claim what the knowledge base
   (`state/kb-context/<key>.md`), `config/cv.json` and `config/profile.md`
   support. If a JD wants something the CV doesn't evidence, leave it out.
2. **Never submit a document that fails the gate.** `check_documents.py` and
   `check_alignment.py` must both print `RESULT: PASS` before any upload. This is
   **enforced in code**: run the pre-submit gate with `--record`, and
   `record_submission.py` refuses to record a `SUBMITTED` row without a fresh,
   hash-matching gate receipt for the exact CV and letter you uploaded.
3. **Eligibility first.** Only apply to roles compatible with the candidate's
   rules in `config/profile.md` (location/work-model, languages, stack). If
   unclear or excluded, record `CLOSED`/`BLOCKED` with the reason and stop.
4. **Email is draft-first and human-sent.** Save a reply with `tools/draft_email.py`;
   the human reviews it in the role drawer and presses **Send with approval**.
   Never volunteer salary, rate, pay or benefits in an email, and never negotiate
   pay in one. If the recruiter asked directly, do not invent a number: leave a
   `[rate to confirm]` placeholder and tell the human. If the candidate says they
   are in other processes, you may add one neutral sentence; never name
   employers, stages or deadlines, and never invent a competing offer. That
   opens the exact email (To/Cc/Subject/body) in an editable dialog: the human can
   amend it before approving, or save changes without sending. Never
   call `gmail_send.py` to send a new email, never send `--to/--body` directly, and
   never set `APPROVE_SEND_EMAIL`, and never call the Gmail API directly: `gmail_send.py`
   requires a saved draft plus a one-time human receipt and refuses otherwise.
   Every send records a dated outbound note with the Gmail message id on the role:
   use a canonical `draft_email.py` draft (`Company:`/`Role:` headers) or pass
   `--company/--role`. `gmail_reconcile.py` also scans Sent as a backstop (notes
   only; it never derives a status from our own email). Calendar writes (`calendar_event.py`) are
   approval-gated the same way (answer the dashboard prompt, set
   `APPROVE_CALENDAR_WRITE=1`, or answer y); reading the calendar and importing an
   `.ics` with `--dry-run` need no approval.
5. **CAPTCHA / 2FA / bot checks.** This build does not solve or evade a
   CAPTCHA. Record `BLOCKED` (or `MANUAL`) with the exact challenge and what you
   tried, and move on. A human can finish the application in their own browser
   with `tools/captcha_manual.sh`. Never solve a 2FA prompt, an email code or a
   login checkpoint yourself, and never work around one. Ask the human for it
   and wait:
   `python3 tools/ask_human.py --mode approve --reason "LinkedIn: approve the
   sign-in on your phone" --detail "<company> / <role>" --timeout 600` pings their
   desktop and shows ONE blocking dialog, then prints
   `{"ok":true,"answer":"approved"}`; use `--mode code` only when the page really
   shows a 6-digit code. A sign-in that needs typing in the page (a Google or
   employer password) is not a code at all: run `tools/open_for_human.py --url
   <login-url> --port <server-port>`, which puts a VISIBLE Camoufox window on that
   worker's port and profile, waits for the human, and leaves it running so the
   application continues in the browser they just used. If no code is emailed, the human supplies the SMS
   code or approves it in their app — do not record `BLOCKED` until the handoff
   has actually timed out or been declined. Email codes are still read with
   `tools/email_verify.py`; only a phone/app step goes to the human.
5b. **Recruitment scams.** Never download or install software for an interview,
   never join a chat-only interview, never share a wallet/seed phrase/private key,
   never pay a fee and never move money. A HIGH signal from
   `tools/scam_check.py` (remote-access tools, wallets, pay-to-work, equipment
   cheques, chat-only interviews) is a wall: record `BLOCKED` with the signal and
   escalate. Do not prepare or submit that role. The dashboard and the Gmail
   review show the warning; see `docs/SCAMS.md`.
6. **Record only with real evidence.** `record_submission.py --evidence` must
   carry the actual thank-you text or confirmation email, never "confirmed"/"ok".
7. **Keep the register current.** It is the single source of truth for resuming.
   Every role has one identity: the queue's `key`, stored in
   `state/applications.csv` (`key`, `apply_url`) and in `state/queue.done`.
   Never key a role by raw company/role text: a rename or a `|` in a company
   name used to create a second, orphaned row. After any reconcile or queue run:
   `python3 tools/register.py --audit` must print `0 problem(s)`; it checks for
   duplicate rows/keys, `queue.done` entries with no register row, SUBMITTED rows
   with no `state/submissions.csv` provenance, a stale `state/counts.md`, a
   PREPARED row whose application email was actually sent with attachments, an
   INTERVIEW row with no invitation in its notes, a live role with no saved job
   description (profile/network rows excepted), and a finished queue row that
   is really a second identity of a register role. `SUBMITTED` is refused
   without a provenance row, and provenance is created by the submission itself:
   `record_submission.py` hashes and snapshots the exact files, verifies the gate
   receipt, then writes the ledger and the status. An approved email carrying
   the CV/letter does the same automatically. The only exemption is a row that
   already carries "provenance not recorded" from `--record-provenance-gaps`; it
   cannot be used as a shortcut on a new claim.
   Repair with `--dedupe` (merge duplicates), `--backfill-done` (record handled
   roles that were never registered), `--record-provenance-gaps` (annotate rows
   that predate provenance logging) and `--backfill` (resync key/apply_url).
   `--stats` writes `state/counts.md`; never edit that file by hand.
8. **Respect each site's terms.** Prefer the employer's own ATS over portals.
   The public build does **not** automate LinkedIn Easy Apply: if a posting only
   offers it, record `BLOCKED` and move on. A private add-on may provide a
   serialised runner, but automating Easy Apply may breach LinkedIn's User
   Agreement; never mass-apply and only use it if the user explicitly enables it.
   Never post, message or interact on social sites unless the user asked in that
   session (and it complies with the site's terms).
9. **Reach outside the repo through the gate.** To read a file outside this repo,
   write a file, or run a shell command, use the gate so the operator can approve
   it: `python3 tools/agent_access.py read <path>` / `write <path>` (content on
   stdin) / `run -- <cmd>`. It asks the operator and only proceeds if they allow
   it (their policy lives in `config/agent-permissions.json`, editable in the
   dashboard's **Settings → Agent permissions**). Native access outside the repo
   is blocked, so this is the only way in; do not try to work around it.
10. **"Skills" means the candidate's job/career skills, not tooling.** When the
   user says they have skills, experience or achievements (from a job, project or
   hobby), capture them as **knowledge-base source documents** in
   `kb/sources/` (grounded, attributed to the employer/project, and honest about
   level) so they flow into the tailored CVs and letters: then re-index. Never
   read "skills" as coding-agent skill packages, plugins, MCP servers or IDE
   extensions unless the user explicitly says their *career* isn't the topic.
   Read their projects/sites through the gate (rule 9) to gather the facts.
11. **Secrets live in the store.** API keys, OAuth client secrets, per-site
    passwords and GraphRAG settings belong in the encrypted store at
    `~/.config/job-search/secrets.json` (AES-256-GCM, key in the OS keyring or a
    0600 key file), managed with `tools/secrets_store.py` and visible in
    **Settings → Secrets**. Never write a secret into `config/`, a tracked
    `.env`, a prompt or a command line. For a site login, ask `python3 tools/accounts.py --get <host>`;
    for an API key, read the environment (the runners inject it) or
    `tools/secrets_store.py --get <section> <name>`.
12. **The browser is Camoufox: never Chromium.** Every browser action goes through
   `tools/camoufox_server.py` + `tools/camoufox_browser.py`. Do **not** use
   Playwright, Chromium, Chrome, headless_shell or pinchtab anywhere in this
   project (applying, verifying, screenshots, testing the dashboard). Playwright's
   Chromium and pinchtab are banned outright; a stray Chromium both breaks the
   browser profile and hogs memory. Parallel applying = one camoufox server per
   agent on its own port (see `state/pipeline-parallel.md`).
13. **Write like a person: no em dashes, no AI slop.** Every word this pipeline
   produces for a human (CVs, letters, emails, briefs, register notes, dashboard
   replies) must be plain English: no em dashes, no "leverage/delve/robust" style
   vocabulary, no "it's worth noting"/"not just X but Y"/"here's the thing",
   no puffery ("a testament to", "pivotal moment"), no weasel attribution
   ("studies show"). Vary sentence length and say the concrete thing. The rule
   has one definition, `tools/writing_style.py`, and it is enforced: the
   pre-submit gate fails a CV or letter that breaks it, and
   `draft_email.py`/the dashboard refuse to save an email draft that breaks it.
   Check any text with `python3 tools/writing_style.py --check <file>`.

## 2a. Delegating work from the dashboard chat

The chat is for conversation and quick checks. When a request is a job of work
(preparing documents, applying, reconciling mail, a discovery sweep, or research
that takes more than a minute), hand it to a background subagent instead of doing it
inside the chat turn:

```bash
python3 tools/delegate.py --title "Short label" --prompt "Full, self-contained task…"
```

It returns immediately with a task id. The subagent runs detached, follows this
file, and appears in the dashboard's **Activity** pane with its own log, so the
chat stays free for the next question. Tell the user it is running and what it
will touch. Keep questions, explanations and one-step answers in the chat. Do not
start a second subagent for the same work: check the Activity pane first.

Multi-role batches go to the queue runner, not the chat: create a scoped queue and
run `tools/run_queue.sh` with `PARALLEL=N` for document preparation. For
submissions that share one ATS account, use `PARALLEL=1`. Parallel browser
sessions on the same account conflict. Do not prepare or submit roles one by one
inside the chat turn.

## 2. Run modes: explain these to the user and let them choose

Do **not** send the user to the documentation. Briefly present the modes below and
ask how they want to run, then do it. Full detail: `docs/RUN-MODES.md`.

**A. Discover** (find roles; apply to nothing)
```bash
python3 tools/discover.py --queue              # LinkedIn job alerts -> queue
python3 tools/email_opportunities.py --apply    # recruiter/contract leads
python3 tools/prioritise_queue.py               # order most-senior-first
```

**B. Review / Prepare** (generate documents, do NOT send, let the user review)
```bash
REVIEW=1 PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh
```
Builds the grounded, targeted CV per role (plus a cover letter only when the advert asks), runs the gates, saves
them under `documents/applications/`, and records `PREPARED`. **Nothing is sent.**

**C. Apply, generated, role-targeted CVs (the default)**
```bash
PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh
```
Per-role generated CV (letter only when required), gate, submit through the employer ATS, record.

**D. Apply with one fixed CV** (fast/cheap; no per-role generation)
```bash
LIGHT=1 FIXED_CV=documents/archetypes/<Prefix>_CV_<Archetype>.docx PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh
```

**E. One role, manually**: follow §4 (for a single URL or a retry).

**F. Submit what's already prepared** (reuse the gated CV/letter, no re-generation)
The dashboard's **🚀 Submit** (grid) / **Submit this application** (a `PREPARED`
row's drawer) build a scoped queue and run `run_queue.sh` in **submit-prepared mode**
(`PREPARED=1`) over just those rows: no GraphRAG, no CV/letter generation, no alignment
gate: only the pre-submit gate (to re-stamp the receipt) and then the browser apply.
Requires `APPROVE_RUN_QUEUE`. Equivalent CLI:

```bash
QUEUE=<tmp-queue> DONE=<tmp.done> PREPARED=1 bash tools/run_queue.sh
```

Common to batch modes:
- Queue file `state/queue.tsv`: `company  role  url  cv-archetype  ats  key`.
- **Most-senior-first** by default (`PRIORITISE=1`); `prioritise_queue.py` sorts the file.
- Reads `config/profile.md`; writes the register + `state/queue.done`; logs to `state/logs/`.
- Watch with `bash tools/watch_queue.sh`; it stops itself on model budget/rate limits.
- **Applying requires a built knowledge base (GraphRAG)**: see §4 step (2) and §5.

So the agent's usual job: fill the queue (§3) → optionally **Review** first →
**Apply** → reconcile (§6).

- From the candidate's inbox: `python3 tools/discover.py` (reads LinkedIn Job

**Every role must have a job description before it enters the queue, and before

`discover.py --queue` refuses to queue a role without one; use `--fetch-jd` (and

## 4. Per-role procedure (this is what each queued job runs)

Given a role (company, role, apply URL, chosen archetype):

A repost is not a blocker. If the same title was applied to before (a repost, or
an earlier application that was rejected), the runner marks it `REPOST` and the
role is prepared/applied again; the grid tags it **repost**. Never record
`CLOSED` merely because a role looks like a duplicate.

```bash
key=<slug-for-this-role>                 # e.g. company-role

# (1) Save the ad text to state/job-descriptions/<key>.md

# (2) Deterministic prep in one command: ATS keywords, GraphRAG (cached by JD
#     hash), archetype selection + alignment, a grounded seed CV pack, and
#     state/briefs/<key>.md (JD + grounded context + paths). It is fast when
#     the JD is unchanged and fails closed on a misaligned archetype.
python3 tools/prepare_role.py --key <key> --company "<Company>" --role "<Role>"

# (3) Read the brief and pack ONCE, then tailor the seed pack with `edit`:
#     profile 150-180 words, tagline, skills, selected work and role bullets.
#     Keep every role and every evidenced achievement; do not rewrite facts.
#     prepare_role wrote state/letters/<key>.need from the advert. Only when it
#     says "required:" write the letter prose to state/letters/<key>.json
#     (headline, title, engagement, opening, fit). Most roles need no letter.
python3 tools/finalise_docs.py --key <key> --company "<Company>" --role "<Role>" \
    --jd state/job-descriptions/<key>.md --ats state/ats/<key>.txt \
    [--engagement contract] [--record-prepared]   # --record-prepared in REVIEW only

# finalise_docs renders the CV (--require-fill), renders the letter only when the
# advert requires one, gates the exact files, and records PREPARED in REVIEW. In
# an apply run it writes the same gate receipt that record_submission.py needs.
# --letter-mode yes forces a letter when the application form demands one.

# (4) Apply via Camoufox through the employer's own ATS
python3 tools/camoufox_server.py --port 9872 &                       # once per session
python3 tools/camoufox_browser.py --server http://127.0.0.1:9872 nav "<apply-url>"
#   ... snap / fill / pick / upload / submit ... (recipes: docs/ATS-RECIPES.md)

# (5) Record the exact files sent (snapshots + hashes) and upsert the register.
#     Add --letter ONLY if that letter exists (the advert or form required one).
python3 tools/record_submission.py --company "<Company>" --role "<Role>" --ats <ATS> \
    --url "<apply-url>" --cv documents/applications/<Prefix>_CV_<key>.docx \
    [--letter documents/applications/<Prefix>_Motivation_<key>.docx] --status SUBMITTED \
    --evidence "<exact thank-you text / confirmation email>"
```

On any failure at (3): fix and re-run, never upload. On a wall at (4): record
`BLOCKED`/`MANUAL` with what you tried and stop.

## 5. Writing the documents (what "good" means)

- **CV** (a *resume*, in US English): mirror the ad's language; include every role and
  every evidenced achievement, with its metrics and technologies; ATS-safe (single
  column for the .docx); fill **both** pages (last page at least 70% full, aim for
  85-95%) without exceeding two. Split compound achievements into separate bullets,
  and give every role a delivery bullet (what shipped, for whom, to what deadline or
  scale) and a team bullet (who you led or coached, how the work kept moving) wherever
  the record supports it - no padding, no invented outcomes. `cv_target.py` prints
  `CONTENT` and `FILL`; the pre-submit gate fails a thin PDF. See `docs/CV-CONTENT.md`.
- **Letter (only when required)**: name the company and role; in the candidate's voice; no shared or
  AI-slop sentences; no duplicated logistics; only claims the CV supports.
- **Grounding**: draw facts from `state/kb-context/<key>.md` (GraphRAG) +
  `config/cv.json` + `config/profile.md`. When the KB says a requirement isn't
  evidenced, do not claim it.
- **Graph hygiene**: after a rebuild run
  `graph_prune_sensitive.py --apply`, `graph_attach_orphans.py --apply` and
  `graph_quality.py --fail-sensitive --fail-orphans`. Never invent a link to
  silence an orphan; add a curated, evidence-backed entry to
  `kb/graphrag/orphan-links.json` instead. Contract/legal material must never
  enter the graph.
- Follow the **accuracy rules** in `config/profile.md` (e.g. certifications on
  the list only; the exact management scope).

## 6. Track replies and interviews

```bash
python3 tools/gmail_reconcile.py            # propose status changes (dry run)
python3 tools/gmail_reconcile.py --apply    # write them; surfaces verification links
bash tools/reconcile_loop.sh                # continuous reconcile + counts
```

- Reconciliation matches mail to register rows and sets `INTERVIEW`/`REJECTED`,
  upgrades `PREPARED`→`SUBMITTED` on confirmation, and prints verification
  links/codes for the **human** to act on (never click/enter them yourself).
- Reconciliation also runs a language-agnostic triage (`tools/email_triage.py`)
  and annotates the review queue. Use the **triage: job-related** filter to find
  job mail the regex put in OTHER. It never changes a status; local domain
  additions live in `config/email-triage.json`.
- **Shelved** is an operator overlay, not a status. `state/shelved.json` holds the keys;
  shelving keeps the register status, notes, documents and provenance unchanged. Do not set a
  status to "shelved"; unshelve from the row menu when the human asks.
- An `action` is a **human to-do** ("reply to Ray about a time", "complete the
  assessment"), never a passive waiting state. Do **not** set "await a reply" (or
  similar): the status and sub-state already say that, and it used to linger
  after the candidate had replied. `register.py` now drops such a phrase, and
  recording a sent reply (`gmail_send.py` / `register.log_outbound`) clears a
  reply/follow-up flag automatically. Clear it yourself with `--action ""` when
  the human has done the thing by hand.
- For interviews: `tools/gmail_calendar_auth.py --check --days N` lists upcoming
  events; `tools/calendar_event.py` creates/updates them (with the interviewer as
  an attendee), imports an `.ics` from a Gmail message and suggests free slots
  (`calendar_event.py slots`) from the real diary. Self-schedule links
  (e.g. Ashby `you.ashbyhq.com/meeting/<id>`) are booked by driving the browser
  like an ATS form. Never guess the candidate's availability: ask, then book.
- **Email is Gmail only**: use `tools/gmail_readonly.py`, `gmail_reconcile.py` and
  `email_opportunities.py`. Never use `mail`, `/var/spool/mail`, or local mailbox
  files; there is no local mail spool. Draft replies with `tools/draft_email.py`
  (never paste a whole email into chat); the dashboard lists them under the role,
  where the human edits and sends with approval. Send only with the human's
  explicit approval.

# Knowledge base (required for targeted documents)

This folder holds the **raw personal documents** the agents are allowed to draw
facts from, and the **GraphRAG index** built from them. It is how you keep CVs,
letters and answers truthful: the agent grounds every claim in this corpus.

It is **required** for document generation: the targeted CVs and letters are written from the cited context pack this produces. (Grounding can fall back to `config/cv.json` only if you truly cannot run GraphRAG.)

**Feed it everything, the more, the better.** The richer the corpus, the sharper
and more honest every application: retrieval can surface the exact achievement,
metric and technology a given ad asks for, with a citation. Do not stop at a CV,
add a master CV, every old/role-specific CV, a brag document with numbers,
project/design notes, talks, reviews, awards, and a LinkedIn export. Keep every
fact traceable to a real experience. **Any format works**: PDF, DOCX, DOC/ODT,
HTML, Markdown, email, CSV/JSON; the ingest step converts it to text for you.
No corpus evidence, no claim.

## Layout

```
kb/
  sources/                 # YOUR documents (text). Put anything here:
                           #   old CVs, a master CV, project notes, product docs,
                           #   a brag/achievements doc, your LinkedIn export, ...
  graphrag/
    settings.example.yaml  # GraphRAG config template -> copy to settings.yaml
    .env.example           # secrets/model config -> copy to .env
    prompts/               # GraphRAG prompts (override to tune extraction)
    input/                 # your sources copied/symlinked here, ready to index
    output/  cache/  logs/ # generated by indexing (git-ignored)
```

## Build it

```bash
# 1. Put your documents in kb/sources/ (any format), then ingest them to text
python3 tools/kb_ingest.py --sources kb/sources --out kb/graphrag/input

# 2. Configure
cp kb/graphrag/settings.example.yaml kb/graphrag/settings.yaml
cp kb/graphrag/.env.example          kb/graphrag/.env      # then edit .env

# 3. Ensure the embeddings backend is up (local llama.cpp by default)
bash tools/embeddings.sh

# 4. Install GraphRAG and build the index (one-off; can take a while)
pip install graphrag          # or use an existing .venv-graphrag
python3 -m graphrag index --root kb/graphrag

# 5. Verify and query
python3 tools/kb_graphrag.py --check
python3 tools/kb_graphrag.py --text "example role, key technologies, metrics"
```

See [docs/KNOWLEDGE-BASE.md](../docs/KNOWLEDGE-BASE.md) for details, embeddings
options, and troubleshooting.

# Adaptive recipes

A recipe is what the adaptive harness learned about one employer's form. It is
declarative JSON, keyed by host and blocker signature, and it is replayed by the
same separate harness, never by the main runner.

Naming: `<host>-<slug>.json`, for example `jobs.example.com-multi-step-wizard.json`.

Every recipe must carry:

- `name`, `host`, `blocker`, `created`, `verified`
- `steps`: a list of `{op, ...}` objects using only the ops in
  `tools/adaptive/validate.py` (`nav`, `fill`, `type`, `select`, `check`,
  `upload`, `press`, `click`, `pick`, `eval`, `waitfor`, `waittext`, `waiturl`,
  `sleep`, `snap`, `text`).

Placeholders `{{email}}`, `{{name}}` and `{{cv}}` are filled by the caller.

Validate before saving or reusing:

```bash
python3 tools/adaptive/validate.py tools/adaptive/recipes/<name>.json
python3 tools/adaptive/validate.py --all
```

A recipe is evidence of a form pattern, not a licence to bypass a control. If
the page shows a CAPTCHA, 2FA, a rate limit, a fee or a payment step, the harness
stops and reports it; no recipe is saved for that.

# Contributing to Jobsquirrel

Thanks for wanting to help. Jobsquirrel is a small, agent-first toolkit; the code is
plain Python + a little shell, with no framework. Contributions that make it
**more accurate**, **more portable** (more countries, languages, ATSes) or
**easier to run as an agent** are especially welcome.

## Ground rules

- **Never add a person-specific or country-specific default.** Everything personal
  belongs in `config/` (git-ignored). No real names, employers, cities, currencies
  or languages may be hard-coded in `tools/`.
- **Truthfulness is a feature.** Don't weaken the gates (`check_documents.py`,
  `check_alignment.py`, `facts.py`). If anything, make them catch more.
- **Keep it agent-drivable.** New behaviour should be a CLI tool + a line in
  `AGENTS.md`/`BOOTSTRAP.md`, not something a human has to click.

## Running it locally

```bash
bash tools/install.sh                 # deps + Camoufox browser + GraphRAG + LibreOffice check
cp config/profile.example.md config/profile.md   # (or let an agent bootstrap you)
cp config/cv.example.json    config/cv.json
cp config/archetypes.example.json config/archetypes.json
python3 tools/build_archetypes.py
```

Use the project venv: `.venv/bin/python tools/<tool>.py`.

## Before you open a PR

- Python: `.venv/bin/python -m py_compile tools/*.py`.
- Shell: `bash -n tools/*.sh install.sh`.
- Tests: `python3 -m pytest -q` (see `tests/`). CI runs these on every PR.
- **No personal or country-specific references** anywhere (your name, your city/
  country, or real employers/clients you used while testing). Check with your own
  terms:
  ```
  grep -rniE "<your-name>|<your-city>|<your-country>|<your-employer>" . | grep -v "\.git/"
  ```
  which must return nothing.
- Don't commit anything under `config/` (your data), `state/`, `documents/` or
  `kb/` (generated/private), they're git-ignored on purpose.

## What's most useful

- **ATS recipes** (`docs/ATS-RECIPES.md`) for systems that don't work yet, or
  fixes for ones that changed.
- **New run modes** or guardrails, always documented in `AGENTS.md`.
- **Portability:** making the eligibility/accuracy rules handle more countries,
  languages and work-authorisation cases.
- **Tests** for the gates (they're the safety net).

## Style

- Small, single-purpose CLI tools in `tools/`; no heavyweight dependencies.
- Comments explain *why*, not *what*. No emojis in code or docs.
- Match the existing structure; prefer editing an existing tool over adding a new one.

## Reporting bugs / ideas

Open an issue with: what you ran, the exact output, and what you expected. If it's
about a specific ATS, include the (public) apply URL and what the form did.

# Account setup
Jobsquirrel · Docs
The pipeline needs a few accounts and credentials. **None are required to read this project**, everything degrades gracefully, but this is the order to set them up so the agent can run the full loop (apply, track replies, verify email). The software (Python deps, the Camoufox browser, GraphRAG, LibreOffice) is fetched by `bash tools/install.sh`; this document covers the accounts and credentials needed on top of that. Secrets live **outside the repo**, in `~/.config/job-search/` by default (override with `GMAIL_CONFIG_DIR` / `ACCOUNTS_FILE`). They are git-ignored. Check the current status at any time: ```bash bash tools/setup_accounts.sh --check ``` The same status, and the Gmail / Google Calendar authorisation flows, are available in the web UI: **Settings → Accounts** (`python3 tools/dashboard.py --open`). The agent will walk you through the steps below either way. --- ## 0. An LLM for the agent (required) You need a capable coding agent and a model key to drive the pipeline (opencode, Claude Code, Cursor, …). If you also use the knowledge base (GraphRAG), it needs its own LLM + embeddings key, see [KNOWLEDGE-BASE.md](KNOWLEDGE-BASE.md). Keep those keys in the central secrets store (**Settings → Secrets**); GraphRAG reads a 0600 mirror at `kb/graphrag/.env`. Never commit them. ## 1. Camoufox browser (required to apply) The submission step drives Camoufox, a Firefox-based browser. ```bash pip install camoufox[geoip] python3 -m camoufox fetch python3 tools/camoufox_server.py --port 9872 & python3 tools/camoufox_browser.py --server http://127.0.0.1:9872 nav https://example.com ``` ## 2. Gmail (recommended, reply tracking + verification) Gmail access lets the pipeline classify confirmations/interviews/rejections, surface **verification links/codes** for you to act on, and (opt-in) send replies with attachments. The token requests `gmail.readonly`, `gmail.send` and `calendar.events`; sending mail and writing to the calendar are still gated on your explicit approval for each action, and the pipeline never deletes mail. Everything here is done from the dashboard: **Settings → Accounts → Google**. 1. **Google Cloud project**: https://console.cloud.google.com → create a project (e.g. `job-pipeline`). **APIs & Services → Library → enable Gmail API** (and Calendar API if you want interview booking). **OAuth consent screen**: User type **External** → Create; app name/support email = your details; **Scopes** → add `gmail.readonly`, `gmail.send` and `calendar.events`; **Test users** → add your own email. Leave it in **Testing** (no Google verification needed for personal use). 2. **OAuth client**: Credentials → Create credentials → **OAuth client ID** → **Desktop app** → Create. 3. **Configure it, then authorise**: either: - paste the **Client ID** and **Client secret** into Settings → Accounts and press **Save Google settings**; the pipeline writes `credentials.json` for you; or - download the JSON and point **credentials** at it in the same panel; or - drop it at the default `~/.config/job-search/credentials.json`. Then press **Authorise Gmail**. A browser opens for consent (first run: `pip install google-auth google-auth-oauthlib google-api-python-client`). The token is saved next to the client (mode 0600) and it also carries the Calendar scope, so one consent covers Gmail **and** Calendar. 4. **Verify**: `python3 tools/gmail_readonly.py --sync` (classifies recent mail), or just **Re-check** in the panel. ### Where the files live (all configurable) Defaults suit most people, but a new user (or a second account) can point the pipeline anywhere. `config/google.json` (see `config/google.example.json`): | key | meaning | | --- | --- | | `config_dir` | folder holding the client/token (default `~/.config/job-search`) | | `credentials` | `credentials.json`, absolute or relative to `config_dir` | | `token` | `token.json`, absolute or relative to `config_dir` | | `client_id` / `client_secret` | paste these in Settings → Accounts; they are stored in the secrets store and `credentials.json` is written from it | Environment overrides win over the file: `GMAIL_CONFIG_DIR`, `GMAIL_CREDENTIALS`, `GMAIL_TOKEN` (and `JOBSQUIRREL_GOOGLE_CONFIG` to relocate `google.json` itself). Check the resolved paths any time: ```bash python3 tools/google_config.py --status # paths, what exists, scopes, account python3 tools/google_config.py --paths # shell-friendly CONFIG_DIR/CREDENTIALS/TOKEN ``` > **Testing-mode tokens expire ~weekly**: re-run `--auth` when that happens. A > Google Workspace account with an *Internal* app avoids it. Optional least-data > tip: create a Gmail filter that labels application mail and set > `GMAIL_QUERY=label:applications`. ### Sending mail (opt-in, attachments supported) Email is **draft-first**. The agent saves a reply with `tools/draft_email.py`; you review it in the role drawer and press **Send with approval**. Only then does the dashboard opens the exact email (To/Cc/Subject/body) in an editable approval dialog. Amend anything, then choose **Approve & send** (a one-time receipt is issued for the edited draft) or **Save changes, don't send**. Attachments are edited in the draft itself. A human at a terminal can still get an explicit preview + y/N prompt. There is no environment-variable bypass: an agent setting `APPROVE_SEND_EMAIL=1` cannot send. Every send is recorded on the role as a dated note with the Gmail message id (use a `draft_email.py` draft or pass `--company/--role`); `gmail_reconcile.py` also scans Sent as a backstop. To enable it, re-authorise including `gmail.send` (the tool's `--auth` uses the scopes in `gmail_readonly.py`). ```bash python3 tools/gmail_send.py --to recruiter@example.com --subject "Application: X" \ --body-file state/draft.txt --signature \ --attach documents/applications/Your_Name_CV_x.docx \ --attach documents/applications/Your_Name_Motivation_x.docx ``` `--attach` is repeatable; a bare filename is also looked up in the configured `attachment_dir`. `--draft state/letters-content/.txt` reads the `To:`/`Subject:`/`Attachment:` header and body straight from a saved draft (CLI flags still override). `--cc`/`--bcc` are supported, and `--dry-run` prints the recipients, attachment names and body without sending. Behaviour lives in `config/email.json` (see `config/email.example.json`): | key | meaning | | --- | --- | | `from` | your address (for reference; Gmail always sends as the token's account) | | `signature` | appended when you pass `--signature` | | `attachment_dir` | fallback directory for relative attachment names | | `max_attachment_mb` | refuse oversized mail before approval (Gmail's limit is 25 MB) | ## 3. Google Calendar (interview booking + tracking) The token includes `calendar.events` (read+write), so the agent can list upcoming interviews, **create/update events** (and invite the interviewer), and **import an `.ics` invite straight from Gmail**: ```bash python3 tools/gmail_calendar_auth.py # requests gmail.readonly + gmail.send + calendar.events python3 tools/gmail_calendar_auth.py --check --days 14 python3 tools/calendar_event.py list --days 14 python3 tools/calendar_event.py create --title "Interview: Acme" \ --start "2026-10-22 14:00" --duration 45 --attendees recruiter@acme.com \ --location "Teams" --description "Interview with the platform team" python3 tools/calendar_event.py from-message # "Add to calendar" for you python3 tools/calendar_event.py slots --days 5 # free slots around your diary ``` `slots` is read-only and proposes interview times inside your working hours without overlapping existing events: pick one, then `create` the event. The same consent as Gmail is all it needs; timezone, default length and working hours come from `config/calendar.json`, editable in Settings → Accounts. Calendar writes are approval-gated: answer `y` at the prompt, approve the dashboard prompt, or set `APPROVE_CALENDAR_WRITE=1` for that one command. `--dry-run` shows the event without writing. `config/calendar.json` (see `config/calendar.example.json`) sets your timezone, default duration, calendar and working hours (the tool warns when a slot falls outside them); `invite_attendees` controls whether attendees also receive an invitation email. ## 4. LinkedIn (optional, manual use) The public build reads LinkedIn job-alert email and can queue those roles, but it does **not** automate LinkedIn Easy Apply. Use the employer's own ATS; if a posting only offers Easy Apply, record `BLOCKED` and apply manually if you choose. You can still log in to LinkedIn manually in the browser for research or a manual application. Never mass-apply, and stop on any CAPTCHA/checkpoint. Automating Easy Apply may breach LinkedIn's User Agreement and can get an account restricted; that capability is a private add-on, not part of this build. ### Persistent sign-in for discovery A host that holds a sign-in can be pinned in `state/browser-affinity.json`: ```json {"linkedin.com": {"port": 9896, "profile": "linkedin"}} ``` The queue runner starts that dedicated profile, routes matching URLs to its port and serialises them, so the sign-in survives across runs. Sign in once on that profile; a login on a worker port is not reused by another port. ## 5. Per-site ATS accounts (Workday, SuccessFactors, Ashby, own sites…) Some applications need an account. `tools/accounts.py` stores a strong password per host (created on first use, 0600, outside the repo): ```bash python3 tools/accounts.py --for https://company.wd3.myworkdayjobs.com/ # get or create python3 tools/accounts.py --list ``` Email verification for these: `python3 tools/email_verify.py --domain [--open]` (reads the newest verification email; never auto-clicks unless you pass `--open` and approve). ## 6. Secrets & privacy - Everything sensitive lives in `~/.config/job-search/`, **outside** the repo: the AES-256-GCM encrypted secrets store (`secrets.json`, 0600, key in the OS keyring or a 0600 `secrets.key`), the `credentials.json` / `token.json` caches Google's libraries read, and the `*-profile/` browser profiles. `accounts.json` is imported into the store and its plaintext backups are folded into an encrypted archive. - `.gitignore` excludes `config/*.md|json` (your data), `state/`, `documents/` generated content, and `kb/` sources/indices. - Revoke access any time: https://myaccount.google.com/permissions. ## Checklist ```bash bash tools/setup_accounts.sh --check # status of every account above ``` | Account | Required? | Verify with | |---|---|---| | LLM key (agent + GraphRAG) | required | the agent runs; `kb_graphrag.py --check` | | Camoufox browser | required to apply | `camoufox_server.py` starts | | Gmail (read-only) | recommended | `gmail_readonly.py --sync` | | Google Calendar | optional | `gmail_calendar_auth.py --check` | | LinkedIn | optional | login persists in the profile | | Per-site credentials | as needed | `accounts.py --list` | ## The secrets store Every secret the app uses has one home: `~/.config/job-search/secrets.json`, AES-256-GCM encrypted, mode 0600 in a 0700 directory, managed from **Settings → Secrets** or: ```bash python3 tools/secrets_store.py --list # masked values only python3 tools/secrets_store.py --check # permissions + syntax python3 tools/secrets_store.py --migrate # import legacy files once printf '%s' "$KEY" | python3 tools/secrets_store.py --set agent OPENROUTER_API_KEY python3 tools/accounts.py --get jobs.example.com python3 tools/accounts.py --for jobs.example.com --email you@example.com # create + store ``` Sections are `agent` (model/API keys), `graphrag` (knowledge-graph LLM), `google` (OAuth client id/secret plus the serialized credential/token files), `accounts` (per-site logins) and `custom`. The dashboard only ever receives masked values. Files that third-party code must read (`credentials.json`, `token.json`, `kb/graphrag/.env`) are regenerated from the store with 0600; they are caches, not the canonical copy. The key is kept in the OS keyring when one is available (Linux Secret Service, macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Locker), otherwise in a 0600 `secrets.key` beside the store. `JOBSQUIRREL_SECRETS_KEY` (base64, 32 bytes) overrides both for CI; the dashboard passes it to its agent children so a locked keyring cannot strand a run. `tools/secrets_store.py --check` reports the encryption and key source without printing either. Existing installs are migrated automatically on the next dashboard start: agent keys leave `agent.json`, the Google client id/secret leave `config/google.json`, `accounts.json` is imported, and plaintext backups (`secrets-backup-*/`, `accounts.json.migrated`, old token copies) are folded into one encrypted archive. `--decrypt-backup FILE` restores such an archive into a private directory if you ever need it.

# Adaptive harness

The main harness is deliberately conservative: one agent, one prompt, one
browser, a fixed set of tools. When it meets a form it does not understand, it
records `BLOCKED` and stops. That is the right default, but it leaves good roles
unsubmitted for a mechanical reason: an unusual widget, an iframe, a wizard, a
file chooser.

The adaptive harness is a **separate** component that takes that one page and
tries to finish it. It does not modify the main harness, and the main harness
does not import it. It is invoked as a black box and returns a JSON result.

```
tools/adaptive/
  AGENT.md          the adaptive agent's manual and hard boundary
  run.sh            launcher: dedicated port/profile, prompt, JSON result
  validate.py       recipe validator (declarative steps only)
  recipes/          verified, reusable form recipes
```

## Separation

| | Main harness | Adaptive harness |
|---|---|---|
| Code | `tools/run_queue.sh`, `tools/agent_run.sh`, prompts | `tools/adaptive/` only |
| Browser | the run's worker port | its own port (`ADAPTIVE_PORT`, default 9899) and profile |
| Writes | register, queue, documents, state | recipes, adapters, `state/logs/adaptive-*` |
| On a wall | records `BLOCKED` and stops | stops and reports the exact wall |
| On success | records the submission | returns the confirmation; the caller records |

The dedicated profile matters: a stuck page in the main worker cannot poison the
adaptive attempt, and a sign-in done in one profile is not silently reused by
the other.

## The boundary

The adaptive harness solves **forms**, not security controls. It must stop and
report, never work around:

- CAPTCHA, hCaptcha, reCAPTCHA, Turnstile, slider or rotate challenges
- 2FA, SMS/authenticator codes, device approvals, login checkpoints
- employer rate limits and application caps
- paywalls, fees, wallets, payment or ID uploads
- site terms that forbid automation

This is the same golden rule as the main harness. A harness that evades those
gets the candidate's accounts banned, and it is not a form problem.

## Running it

```bash
ADAPTIVE=1 PARALLEL=1 bash tools/run_queue.sh
```

With `ADAPTIVE=1`, a task that comes back `BLOCKED` is handed to the adaptive
harness on its own browser. If the harness returns a verified confirmation, the
caller records `SUBMITTED` with that text as evidence. If it returns a wall, the
row stays `BLOCKED` with the exact reason.

Run it directly for one role:

```bash
bash tools/adaptive/run.sh \
  --company "Acme" --role "Staff Engineer" \
  --url "https://jobs.example.com/apply" \
  --cv documents/applications/Acme_CV_staff.docx \
  --key acme-staff \
  --blocker "unknown multi-step wizard"
```

It prints one JSON line:

```json
{"ok":true,"confirmation":"Thank you for applying","recipe":"tools/adaptive/recipes/...","notes":"..."}
```

or

```json
{"ok":false,"blocker":"exact wall text","url":"...","notes":"..."}
```

## Recipes

When the harness solves a form, it writes a recipe under
`tools/adaptive/recipes/`. A recipe is a declarative list of browser steps
(`nav`, `fill`, `upload`, `click`, `waittext`, ...) with `{{email}}`, `{{name}}`
and `{{cv}}` placeholders. It is validated by `tools/adaptive/validate.py` and
replayed by the adaptive harness on the same host. It is never imported by the
main harness and it cannot contain shell or filesystem code.

A recipe is only saved after it has been tested on the page. A failed attempt
leaves no recipe behind.

# Driving the pipeline with an AI agent

This project is built to be **run by an AI coding agent**, not clicked through by
hand. The intended workflow is: a human fills in `config/`, then points an agent
(opencode, Claude Code, Cursor, …) at the repository and tells it what to do. The
agent then discovers roles, tailors documents, gates them, and applies, you just
review and make the few calls only a human should.

`AGENTS.md` (repo root) is the agent's operating manual and is read automatically
by opencode and similar tools. This document is the human's guide to handing the
project over.

> **New here?** See **[docs/AGENT-SETUP.md](AGENT-SETUP.md)** for the exact
> commands per agent (opencode, Claude Code, Cursor, …), how to keep the running
> cost low with opencode + DeepSeek Flash, and what it typically costs.
>
> **This is not push-button autonomy.** The agent does the mechanical work and
> relies on the instructions in `AGENTS.md`; you make the judgement calls
> (your rules, approving emails, solving CAPTCHA/2FA).

## 1. One-time setup (human)

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt && python3 -m camoufox fetch
cp config/profile.example.md      config/profile.md          # your identity + rules
cp config/cv.example.json         config/cv.json             # your CV as data
cp config/archetypes.example.json config/archetypes.json     # your CV templates
python3 tools/build_archetypes.py                            # build the archetypes
# Gmail (read-only) is optional; the knowledge base (GraphRAG) is required, docs/KNOWLEDGE-BASE.md
```

That is the only manual work. Everything after this is the agent.

## 2. Hand it to the agent

Give the agent the repository path and a brief like:

> You are operating my job-search pipeline (this repo). Read `AGENTS.md` and
> `config/profile.md` first. Then:
> 1. Find new senior roles and add them to `state/queue.tsv`.
> 2. Run the pipeline (`PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh`).
> 3. Reconcile with my email and tell me what needs me.
> Only apply to roles that fit my eligibility and accuracy rules. Never send
> email without asking me. Stop on any CAPTCHA/2FA.

Because `AGENTS.md` is auto-loaded, most agents will already know the procedures;
the brief above just sets the goal.

On first run the agent opens by reading **`docs/INTRO.md`** to the user, a plain
language overview of what the pipeline is, how it works, the run modes, and their
privacy, before it starts the interview.

## 3. What the agent does autonomously vs escalates

**Autonomous**
- Discover roles (`discover.py`, `email_opportunities.py`, or web search) and queue them.
- Save ads, extract ATS keywords, build the grounded context pack.
- Choose and verify the aligned CV archetype; write the targeted CV + letter.
- Run the pre-submit gate; fix and re-run until it passes.
- Drive the browser (Camoufox) through the employer ATS and submit.
- Record provenance and upsert the register; reconcile email and set statuses.

**Escalate to you (it must stop and ask / record BLOCKED/MANUAL)**
- CAPTCHA / 2FA / bot checks ("suspicious activity").
- Any email to be **sent** (recipient + subject + content need your approval).
- Verification links/codes to be clicked/entered (it surfaces them only).
- Ambiguous eligibility/accuracy rules, missing `config/`, or a corrupt register.

## 4. The two ways it works

- **Batch**: fill `state/queue.tsv`, then `bash tools/run_queue.sh`. One
  sub-agent per role does the full procedure. Processes **most senior first**.
- **Per role**: the agent runs the same steps for a single job (useful for a
  retry, a specific URL, or showing you a CV before applying).

Both are described step-by-step with exact commands in `AGENTS.md` §3-§6 and
`docs/WORKFLOW.md`.

## 5. A worked exchange

```
You:  Find and queue new senior roles, then run the pipeline.
Agent: [discover.py + web search] queued 6 roles (Director, 3× EM, 2× Staff).
       [run_queue.sh] Acme Head of AI SUBMITTED · Beta CLOSED (dead
       posting) · Aon BLOCKED (hCaptcha, needs you) ... 
       Register: 120 SUBMITTED · 5 INTERVIEW · 8 REJECTED · 2 BLOCKED.
       Needs you: solve the Aon hCaptcha; approve a reply to ATG.

You:  Reconcile with email.
Agent: [gmail_reconcile.py --apply] set 1 INTERVIEW, 2 REJECTED; verification
       links surfaced for 3 applications.
```

## 6. Notes

- **Monitoring:** watch a run live with `bash tools/watch_queue.sh`; the raw log is
  `state/logs/run_queue.out`; progress/status via `python3 tools/register.py --stats`
  and `bash tools/reconcile_loop.sh`. See **[USING-IT.md](USING-IT.md)** for typical
  prompts and what to watch.
- **Model budget:** `run_queue.sh` stops itself on model rate/budget limits and
  tells you; top up and re-run.
- **Rate limits / anti-bot:** the pipeline is deliberately polite (one submission
  at a time for LinkedIn, back-off on 429s). Do not ask the agent to hammer a site.
- **Human steps are real:** some employers genuinely require a human CAPTCHA/2FA
  pass. The system routes those to `state/queue-human.tsv` and `human_assist.sh`.
- **Accuracy is the point:** if the agent can't evidence a claim, it leaves it
  out. Lower ATS coverage is acceptable; a fabrication is not.

# Bootstrap it with your AI agent: and what it costs

This project has no installer wizard and no GUI. You hand the repository to an
AI coding agent, and **the agent sets the whole thing up with you**: it reads you
the introduction, interviews you, writes your `config/`, builds your CV
archetypes, builds your knowledge base, and sets up your accounts, explaining
each step in plain language.

You do **not** need to read the other docs to get started. The agent reads them
for you. This page just tells you how to launch an agent against the repo, how to
keep the running cost low, and how the cost works.

---

## 0. Read this first: it is not push-button autonomy

Be realistic about what this is:

- **It relies on instructions.** The behaviour lives in `AGENTS.md` and
  `BOOTSTRAP.md`. The agent is only as good as (a) the model driving it and (b)
  how accurately you filled in `config/`. A weak model or a sloppy config gives
  weak results.
- **It is not fully autonomous.** The agent does the mechanical work, find,
  tailor, gate, submit, record, reconcile, but **you** make the judgement calls
  and handle the human-only moments: your eligibility/accuracy rules, approving
  any email before it is sent, and solving CAPTCHA/2FA when an employer demands
  it. Some employers genuinely require a person.
- **You supervise the first run.** Treat the first role or two as a supervised
  trial: review the generated CV and letter, and confirm the gates behaved.
- **You are responsible for what it sends.** It is built never to fabricate and
  never to send a document that fails the gate, but you own your applications.

If you want a one-click, unattended "AI applies to 500 jobs" bot: this is not
that, and you should be wary of anything that claims to be.

---

## 1. Run it with opencode (recommended, and the cheapest to run)

[opencode](https://opencode.ai) auto-loads `AGENTS.md`, so it already knows the
procedures before you say anything. **You don't even need to clone the repo**,
the agent can do that too.

```bash

```

First time only, connect a model provider:

```text

/models      # pick a DeepSeek model (see §3)
```

Then paste this single prompt, that is the entire installation:

```text
Clone https://github.com/bongomanuk/jobsquirrel.git into ./jobsquirrel and set it
up with me: read AGENTS.md, read docs/INTRO.md to me, then run the first-run
bootstrap in BOOTSTRAP.md.
```

The agent clones the repo, installs the dependencies, walks you through the
interview, builds your config + archetypes + knowledge base, and sets up your

applying.

If you already cloned it, just `cd jobsquirrel`, run `opencode`, and say:
*"Read AGENTS.md, introduce the project, and run the bootstrap."*

You can also pin the model in `opencode.json` (or `opencode.jsonc`) at the repo
root so the agent always starts on a cheap model:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash"
}
```

---

## 1b. Choose the model (works for every agent)

The **Agent console header** has a model picker (the same idea as opencode's
`/model`), and **Settings → AI & agent** has the same list. The list comes from
the selected CLI (`opencode models`, or Claude Code's aliases), grouped by product
(**Free models**, **OpenCode Zen**, **OpenCode Go**, **Contributor / preview**, or
**Claude Code**); the group is the provider prefix, and free models are pulled out
so they are easy to find. Anything else can be typed in the free-text box.

Both write `~/.config/job-search/agent.json`:

```jsonc
{
  "agent": "",                    // "" = auto-detect (opencode, else claude)
  "model": "opencode/claude-haiku-4-5",
  "models": {                     // remembered choice per agent
    "opencode": "opencode/claude-haiku-4-5",
    "claude": "sonnet"
  },
  "env": { "OPENCODE_API_KEY": "..." }
}
```

- `tools/agent_run.sh` reads this file itself, so the selection applies to **chat,
  role chats, queue/apply runs and every API/CLI-invoked task** that goes through
  the runner.
- Environment overrides win for one run: `MODEL=... AGENT=... bash tools/run_queue.sh`.
- A custom agent command receives the chosen model in `$MODEL` (it decides how to
  pass it on). opencode gets `--model`, Claude Code gets `--model`.
- **Transient provider failures are retried.** A 420/429/5xx, "rate limit", "too
  many requests" or "quota exceeded" failure is retried up to **4** times with
  exponential backoff (20s base, plus jitter). opencode retries continue the same
  session, so a failure midway through a task does not repeat the tool calls
  already made; a custom agent without a resumable session is only retried when
  it has not acted yet. `AGENT_RETRY=0` disables it, `AGENT_RETRY_BASE=<seconds>`
  changes the backoff. A task that succeeds after a retry keeps its STATUS and is
  not treated as an infrastructure stop.
- The **GraphRAG LLM is separate** (`kb/graphrag/.env`, **Settings → GraphRAG**): the
  knowledge-graph builder does not use the coding-agent model.

### OpenRouter models

**Settings → AI & agent → Main agent → OpenRouter** reveals the OpenRouter key
field and its model list (grouped by provider, with free models separated). Pick
a model or type its id; the model picker and provider settings save immediately.

The key is stored in the encrypted secrets store (`~/.config/job-search/secrets.json`),
never in the repository. OpenCode remains the local tool runner (it reads `AGENTS.md`
and drives the browser/commands); OpenRouter supplies the model. The non-secret
selection in `~/.config/job-search/agent.json` looks like:

```jsonc
{
  "agent": "openrouter",
  "model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
  "models": { "openrouter": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash" }
}
```

`tools/agent_run.sh` forwards the key to the runner and prefixes the model with
`openrouter/` for OpenCode. Queue/apply runs, chat and role chats all use it.

### Give subagents their own provider and model

The dashboard runs document preparation and delegated background tasks as
**subagents**. In **Settings → AI & agent → Subagents** choose *Same as main
agent* (the default) or a different provider and model. Provider keys and
endpoints are shared, so a second provider only needs its key entered once. The
saved selection adds two keys:

```jsonc
{
  "agent": "opencode",
  "model": "inferx/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-basic",
  "subagent_agent": "openrouter",
  "subagent_model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash"
}
```

- An empty `subagent_agent` follows the main agent; an empty `subagent_model`
  follows the main model (or uses the subagent provider's saved/default model).
- Submissions, the chat and role chats stay on the **main agent**. Subagents are
  the dashboard's document-preparation and background runs.
- `PARALLEL` (1–6) is set on the same panel; submissions always run one at a time.

### Run it fully local

The pipeline does not need a cloud model. `tools/agent_run.sh` accepts any
OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint as the agent model: **llama.cpp**
(`llama-server`), **Ollama**, **LM Studio**, **vLLM** or another
OpenAI-compatible server.

Set the agent to `local` (or `llamacpp`) and point it at the server:

```jsonc
{
  "agent": "local",
  "model": "local/qwen2.5-coder-32b-instruct",
  "models": { "local": "local/qwen2.5-coder-32b-instruct" },
  "env": {
    "LOCAL_LLM_BASE_URL": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1",
    "LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY": "sk-local"
  }
}
```

Or for one run:

```bash
AGENT=local MODEL=local/qwen2.5-coder-32b-instruct \
LOCAL_LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 bash tools/run_queue.sh
```

- The **GraphRAG** completion model is separate: point `GRAPHRAG_API_BASE`,
  `GRAPHRAG_API_KEY` and `GRAPHRAG_LLM_MODEL` in `kb/graphrag/.env` at the same
  local server. Embeddings already run locally (`tools/embeddings.sh`).
- The browser (Camoufox), CV/letter rendering (LibreOffice), register, dashboard
  and knowledge graph are all local. Apart from the employer's site and
  Gmail/Calendar (both optional), the model endpoint is the only thing that
  would otherwise leave the machine.

  frontier model. Start with REVIEW runs (`REVIEW=1`) and supervise the first

### Running the queue with Claude Code

The queue runner starts one headless agent per role through
`tools/agent_run.sh`. It uses opencode if that is installed, otherwise Claude
Code; `AGENT=claude` picks Claude Code explicitly:

```bash
AGENT=claude REVIEW=1 PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh    # prepare only
AGENT=claude PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh             # apply
AGENT=claude MODEL=sonnet PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh
```

Sign in to the `claude` CLI first (run `claude` once in a terminal). If it is
signed out, the runner records "agent not signed in" and stops after three
failed tasks; nothing is lost and the roles stay pending.

A headless run cannot stop and ask you to approve a tool, so each task may use
only what the role needs: reading and writing files in the repo, web search and
fetch (to find the employer's own apply page), and the pipeline's Python tools.
Anything else is refused. No MCP servers are loaded, so mail and social tools
you have connected elsewhere are out of reach. This is a guardrail, not a
sandbox: `python3` can still do anything. To change it:

| Env | Effect |
|---|---|
| `CLAUDE_ALLOWED_TOOLS="..."` | replace the allowlist (space-separated rules, e.g. `Read Edit Bash(python3 *)`) |
| `CLAUDE_PERMISSION_MODE=bypassPermissions` | allow every tool (not recommended) |
| `CLAUDE_ARGS="--max-turns 80"` | extra flags for every task, e.g. `--no-session-persistence` to keep the runs out of your session history |

The same mechanism runs any other CLI agent: `AGENT="mycli run"` runs
`mycli run "<prompt>"` for each role. `AGENT` applies to `run_queue.sh`
and `human_assist.sh` alike.

### macOS

Everything runs on macOS as well as Linux. macOS ships without GNU `flock`,
`setsid` and `timeout`, so `tools/compat/` provides portable stand-ins. The
runners append that directory to `PATH` (after the system directories, so a real
command always wins where one exists) and bake the resolved `timeout` path into
each task prompt, so the agent uses the same one. The stand-ins are self-contained
Python and are covered by `tests/test_compat.py`.

| `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash` |    $0.30 |       $1.20 |          $0.006 | ~$0.03-0.10                  |
| `opencode/deepseek-v4-pro`   |      $1.74 |       $3.48 |          $0.145 | ~$0.15-0.60                  |

*(List prices are OpenCode's published rates and change over time; the provider
also offers a free `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free` variant for a limited
period. Check the console for current prices.)*

**How to keep it cheap**

- **Pick a Flash model.** `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash` is the default
  recommendation; drop to `deepseek-v4-flash` for lots of volume.
- **Let caching work.** Inputs are mostly repeated context (system prompt,
  `AGENTS.md`, the growing turn history); cached reads are ~50× cheaper than
  fresh input, so keep long-lived sessions in one thread instead of restarting.
- **Prefer LIGHT / REVIEW modes while tuning.** `REVIEW=1` (build + gate only, no
  submit) and `LIGHT=1 FIXED_CV=…` (one CV, no per-role generation) cost far less
  than full per-role generation.
- **Set a spend limit.** OpenCode Console (pay-as-you-go) lets you cap monthly
  usage and control auto-reload. A $20 balance goes a long way for this pipeline.
- **Don't paste the resume into a paid chat.** Use the tools; they keep context
  small and cached.
- **Batch in one session.** Discovery → queue → apply → reconcile in a single
  agent session shares the cached context.

---

## 4. How much it typically costs to run

Rough, order-of-magnitude figures, **not a quote.** Your real spend depends on
the model, how many turns the browser driving takes, and how many retries happen.

Assumptions for one full **apply** run (one role, end to end):

- ~150k-600k input tokens, **mostly cache reads** (the system prompt + history
  are re-sent each turn);
- ~10k-40k output tokens (the CV content, the letter, browser actions);
- discovery, email reconciliation, and chatting with the agent are separate and
  small.

With those assumptions:

| What                              | DeepSeek V4.1 Flash      |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| One application (apply mode)      | ~$0.03-0.10 (≈$0.05 typ.) |
| 50 applications                   | ~$2-5                    |
| 100 applications                  | ~$3-10                   |
| A month of active use + chatting  | ~$5-15 total             |

- **DeepSeek V4 Flash** cuts those roughly in half.
- **DeepSeek V4 Pro** is ~4-6× the price of V4.1 Flash, reserve it for hard
  cases.
- **Review/Prepare mode** (no browser, no submit) is the cheapest useful run.
- If you run a lot, a flat monthly subscription (OpenCode **Go**, $10/month)
  can be cheaper than pay-as-you-go, see the OpenCode console.

The honest summary: for a normal job search this costs **single-digit dollars a
month** on a Flash model. The expensive failure modes are a bad model looping on
the browser and unbounded retries, so set a spend cap.

---

## 5. What the agent will ask you (so you're ready)

On the first run the agent interviews you. Have these to hand:

- Your CV (a file) and any "brag"/project documents you want the knowledge base
  to learn from.
- Where you can work and what you'll accept (locations, remote/hybrid/on-site,
  work authorisation, languages, contract vs permanent).
- Availability and pay expectations.
- The **accuracy rules**: claims you must never overstate (titles, scope,
  certifications, metrics).
- Optional: read-only Gmail and a one-time LinkedIn login for reply tracking and
  manual use. The public build does not automate Easy Apply.

Then it builds everything and shows you the run modes (**Discover / Review /
Apply / fixed-CV**) so you can choose.

# Architecture
Jobsquirrel · Docs
## Shape A set of small, single-purpose CLI tools (Python + a few shell scripts) that share three things: the **config** (`config/`), the **register** (`state/applications.csv`) and the **provenance ledger** (`state/submissions.csv`). The runner (`tools/run_queue.sh`) orchestrates them per job by spawning an AI coding agent whose instructions are generated from the config, so all the "knowledge" lives in config + data, not in the scripts. ``` config/profile.md ─┐ config/cv.json ───┼─> cv_builder ─> archetypes ─> cv_target/letter ─> GATE ─> ATS (browser) ─> record config/archetypes.json ┘ check_alignment / check_documents │ ▼ inbox <─ gmail_readonly/gmail_reconcile ── register (applications.csv) <── submissions.csv ``` ## Configuration (the only person-specific inputs) | File | What it holds | |---|---| | `config/profile.md` | Identity, work authorisation, languages, availability, pay, **eligibility** and **accuracy** rules, EEO answers. Read as `- key: value`. | | `config/cv.json` | The CV as data: `experience[]`, `projects[]`, `skills[]`, `education[]`, `certifications[]`, `languages[]`, `sidebar{}`. Ground truth for the gate. | | `config/archetypes.json` | Role-family templates: `{key,title,headline,tagline,opening,profile,fit,skills,tags}`. | If `config/profile.md` / `cv.json` / `archetypes.json` are absent, the tools fall back to the matching `*.example.*` file, so the project runs out of the box with placeholder data. ## Data model **`state/applications.csv`**: the canonical outcome register, one row per role: `date, company, role, ats, status, letter, notes, employment, action, key, apply_url`. **`key`** is the role's single identity (the queue row's last column); `queue.done` stores the same key and `apply_url` is the apply target, so a rename or a `|` in a company name can never create a second, orphaned row. Rows written before that column existed fall back to `company|role`. Statuses: `QUEUED, PREPARED, IN_PROGRESS, SUBMITTED, INTERVIEW, OFFER, REJECTED, BLOCKED, MANUAL, CLOSED` (`PREPARED` = documents built and gated, nothing sent). The application process is a **state machine**: this one `status` is the machine stage, every tool transitions it, and the dashboard renders the same machine. Managed by `tools/register.py`: read with `--stats/--list/--show`, edit with `--set/--render/--delete`, and **audit** with `--audit` (exits non-zero on a duplicate row or key, a `queue.done` entry with no row, a `SUBMITTED` row with no provenance, a stale `state/counts.md`, a PREPARED row whose application email was actually sent with attachments, an INTERVIEW row with no invitation in its notes, a live role with no saved job description, or a finished queue alias of a register row). `record_submission.py` and the pre-submit gate both refuse a SUBMITTED row without the saved advert (`--no-jd` is the explicit exception for a network profile). `SUBMITTED` is refused without provenance, which is written by the submission action itself (hash, snapshot, gate receipt, then ledger + status); an application email does the same automatically. Repair with `--dedupe`, `--backfill`, `--backfill-done` and `--record-provenance-gaps`; `--stats` regenerates `state/counts.md`, which is never edited by hand. **`state/submissions.csv`**: the provenance ledger: the exact files sent per application, with `sha256` and a snapshot directory under `documents/submitted/`. Written by `tools/record_submission.py` (which also upserts the register). **Queues**: `state/queue.tsv` tab-separated: `company role url cv-archetype ats key`. `run_queue.sh` processes rows whose `key` is not in `state/queue.done`, **most-senior-first** by default (`PRIORITISE=1`; set `PRIORITISE=0` for file order). `tools/prioritise_queue.py` sorts the queue file itself by seniority. ## Tools by role - **Build**: `cv_builder.py` (library), `build_archetypes.py`, `cv_target.py`, `cv_fill.py`, `make_letter.py`, `fix_letterheads.py`. - **Gate**: `check_alignment.py` (role family ↔ CV), `check_documents.py` (pre-submit), `ats_keywords.py` (coverage), `facts.py` (claim/tense checks), `gate_receipt.py` (hash-stamped PASS receipts; `record_submission.py` refuses a `SUBMITTED` row without one), `jd_guard.py` (a role needs a saved job ad before it is queued). - **Record**: `register.py`, `record_submission.py`, `outcomes.py`. - **Email**: `gmail_readonly.py`, `gmail_reconcile.py`, `email_triage.py` (language-agnostic review hints), `gmail_calendar_auth.py`, `gmail_send.py`, `discover.py`, `email_opportunities.py`, `email_verify.py`. - **Browser**: `camoufox_server.py`, `camoufox_browser.py`, `camoufox_test.py`. - **Run**: `run_queue.sh` (parallel queue), `agent_run.sh` (whichever agent CLI you have), `reconcile_loop.sh`, `watch_queue.sh`, `build_human_queue.py`, `human_assist.sh`, `captcha_manual.sh`, `chain_queue.sh`, `requeue_blocked.sh`. - **Approval and access**: `approval.py` (risky actions), `send_receipt.py` (one-time human receipts for a specific send), `agent_access.py` (the gate for anything outside the repo: read, write, run). - **Grounding (required)**: `kb_graphrag.py` (+ `kb/`), `embeddings.sh`, `graph_explore.py` (read the index), `ontology.py` (+ `config/ontology.example.json`), `web/graph3d.js` (the Three.js Knowledge workspace). - **Secrets**: `secrets_store.py` (encrypted 0600 store; OS keyring or key file), `accounts.py`, `google_config.py`, `diagnostics` via `doctor.py`. ## Knowledge workspace The top-bar **Knowledge** page is a full-page Three.js view over the same GraphRAG index. `graph_explore.py` exposes the Universe, ontology aggregates, the community hierarchy, connected entity subgraphs, ego networks, semantic search, role evidence and cited answers; `graph_importance.py` scores entities by weighted message passing; `graph_universe.js` and `graph3d.js` are the Universe and Map renderers, and `web/app.js` owns the node pane, focus/fade, Ask, enrichment and edit flows. Overlays (`enrichment.json`, `edits.json`, `orphan-links.json`) are merged at read time so they survive a rebuild. `ontology.py` maps GraphRAG types to the classes shown in `config/ontology.example.json`. The frontend owns the scene, orbit/zoom/pan, raycast and HTML hotspots; `dashboard.py` owns the breadcrumbs, search, source management and role links. Orphans are attached with evidence-backed overlay links; anything that cannot be honestly linked is grouped in the labelled *Unlinked evidence* island instead of floating among the themes. The **Roles** tab in the workspace is the bridge to applications: it lists register rows and opens one in the existing job drawer, or prepares a queued role. The ontology's `REQUIRES` / `SATISFIES` vocabulary is the place to grow role-to-evidence edges without changing the graph renderer. ## Machine-local state and compression Everything the pipeline learns about a run lives in `state/` and is machine-local. It is largely text: saved job ads, ATS keyword files, GraphRAG grounding packs, CV content packs, letters, gate receipts, agent transcripts: so it compresses 3-7x, and `tools/storage.py` packs the cold parts: | Area | Action | Read back by | |---|---|---| | logs idle for a day | `--logs`, plus `--pack-log ` the moment a role finishes | the dashboard reads `.gz` directly | | per-role artifacts older than `--state-days` | `--state` | `tools/stateio.py` | | `state/gmail_cache.json` | `--gmail-cache` | `gmail_reconcile.py` | | `kb/graphrag/cache` | `--graphrag-cache --apply` (tar.zst archive) | re-extract if you want incremental indexing | The invariant is that **a packed artifact is indistinguishable from a plain one**: `stateio.resolve()` returns `x` or `x.gz`, `read_text()` reads either, and `ensure()` restores one in place (keeping its original mtime) when a tool needs a real file. A queue run hydrates everything at the start (`--hydrate-all`) and packs the cold leftovers when it finishes. Never packed: files that are appended to or written by shell redirection (`queue*.tsv`, `*.done`, `*.csv`, `state/drafts/`, live dashboard logs), symlinks, and, by default, anything git tracks (packing a tracked file is a deletion plus an untracked `.gz`; `--include-tracked` overrides). `documents/` holds `.docx` and `.pdf`, already-compressed containers; `kb/graphrag/output/` is read at query time and stays unpacked. Details: **[STORAGE.md](STORAGE.md)**. ## Runner model `run_queue.sh` spawns `PARALLEL` workers; each pops the next pending queue row and runs the configured agent (`agent_run.sh`: opencode, Claude Code or any CLI) with a generated prompt. On macOS the runner falls back to the portable `flock`, `setsid` and `timeout` stand-ins in `tools/compat/`. The prompt (built from `config/`) tells the agent to: read `config/profile.md`; apply the eligibility gate; choose and verify the aligned archetype; build a targeted CV + letter; pass the pre-submit gate; submit through the employer ATS via `camoufox_browser.py`; and record the result. One queue slot = one application. Blocked/closed roles are recorded with a reason; the runner never fabricates a submission. ## Knowledge base (GraphRAG) `kb/sources/` (your CVs, notes, product docs) is indexed by Microsoft GraphRAG into `kb/graphrag/`. `kb_graphrag.py` then builds a cited grounding pack per role into `state/kb-context/`, which the agent uses as the single source of truth for achievements and metrics. This is **required** for document generation: the targeted CVs and letters are written from it.
