# How Cascade is integrated

The dashboard uses **[Cascade](https://github.com/erobwen/liquefy)**, the reactive
UI framework by **Robert Renbris**, for its dynamic surfaces. This page is the
map of that integration: what is on Cascade, how the vanilla application talks to
it, and what deliberately stays outside it.

Cascade is licensed under the ISC License; the vendored copy's notice and
package versions are in `tools/web/vendor/cascade.NOTICE`. See also
[Credits](CREDITS.md).

## The bundle and the islands

The dashboard is still served as static files with no build step. Cascade is
vendored once as a browser ESM bundle:

- `tools/web/vendor/cascade.js` is built with esbuild from
  `@liquefy/cascade.reactive`, `.component`, `.dom` and the overlay part of
  `.ui`, currently the 3.x line. The exact entry and versions are in
  `vendor/cascade.NOTICE`.
- `tools/web/cascade-islands.js` imports that bundle and mounts the islands.
- `tools/dashboard.py` serves and fingerprints both files, and reloads an open
  tab when they change.

An **island** is a small Cascade component tree rendered onto one existing DOM
element. The rest of the page remains the application's own JavaScript. Each
island has a tiny API on `window.CascadeIslands`, and the vanilla side calls it
with a plain view model. If the module is unavailable, the old markup is used or
the original controls are revealed.

The grid's aggregate model is a Cascade **store** rather than a component tree.
`tools/web/grid-stats.js` derives the bucket, status, sub-state, shelved and
scam counts in one pass; `cascade-islands.js` wraps that derivation in one
`observable` and exposes it as `CascadeIslands.stats`. `app.js` publishes the
raw rows after each `/api/grid` load and reads the snapshot for the bucket
chips, the state map, the tooltips and the sub-state filter. There is no second
count derivation for those surfaces to drift from.

## Signals in Cascade 3

Cascade 3 splits the signal API in two. Ordinary state uses `observable`, while
the framework's render targets use `temporal`. Only a render target needs a
temporal signal; data, stores and component state are plain observables. That is
why the bundle exports both, and why `cascade-islands.js` creates its stores with
`observable`: the components it builds already sit on temporal render targets
provided by Cascade.

The split is a major version because code written for Cascade 2 could use
`observable` everywhere. When a surface is ported or a new island is added, use
`observable` for the data it holds and let Cascade own the temporal side. Do not
wrap a store in `temporal` just to make a component update.

## Off-screen pages

Cascade can keep a page alive while it is off screen, which makes page swaps
nearly instant. That needs the page itself to be a Cascade component wrapped in
the framework's page container. The dashboard is still a single document with
islands, so it does not use that yet; the islands get the same benefit on their
own surfaces through `flipAnimationContainer`. If the dashboard moves to
Cascade-owned pages, this is the first optimisation to take.

## What each island covers

| Surface | Components | Cascade features | The vanilla side |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Activity run roster | `ActivityRoster` | component state, `flipAnimationContainer` | computes the roster from the live run and calls `CascadeIslands.activity.set(view)` |
| Grid rows | `GridRows`, `RawRow` | custom `DOMNodeComponent`, keyed rows, `flipAnimationContainer` with `display: contents` so rows stay real `<tr>` elements | filters, sorts, groups and selection still compute the row models |
| Grid aggregate model | `CascadeIslands.stats` (`observable`) | one reactive store over the pure `grid-stats.js` derivation | publishes `GRID` and the bucket classifier; reads counts for the chips, state map, tooltips and sub-state filter |
| Role drawer | `DrawerTabs`, `DrawerBody`, `RawBlock` | state-driven tabs, raw block for the existing tab HTML | the seven tab renderers and their actions |
| Grid toolbar | `ToolbarExtra` | `overflowContainer`, `elementSlot`, `elementBoundsProvider` | the original buttons stay hidden as the click handlers |
| Knowledge search results | `KgResults` | keyed result components, `flipAnimationContainer` | search and graph navigation |
| Knowledge side tabs | `KgTabs` | state-driven tabs | the tab content |
| Context menu | `CtxMenuRoot` | `overlayFrame`, `overlay`, nested submenus | `App.rowMenu` still builds the item model and actions |
| Role URLs and page title | module-level router and head | `browserLocation`, `documentHead` | row opening/closing and the page title text |

## Data flow

The application owns the data. A typical update looks like this:

1. The vanilla code fetches or computes something (a run roster, grid row
   models, the current drawer tab).
2. It calls the island's small API, for example
   `CascadeIslands.grid.set(models)` or `CascadeIslands.activity.set(view)`.
3. Cascade diffs the component tree and patches only the nodes that changed.
   `flipAnimationContainer` animates elements that move, appear or leave.

The islands never fetch. They receive plain data and callbacks, so the
application's permissions, state and rendering rules stay in one place.

The aggregate model follows the same rule. `grid-stats.js` is a pure function
over rows and a bucket classifier; the Cascade store only holds its latest
snapshot. A filter keystroke does not recompute it. A new `/api/grid` response
does, once, and every surface reads the same numbers.

## What stays outside Cascade

- **The 3D graph canvases.** The map and universe views are Three.js renderers
  with their own layout and input. Cascade owns the surrounding search results
  and tabs, not the canvas.
- **The row list pipeline.** `GRID`, filtering, sorting, grouping, selection and
  the register remain the existing JavaScript engine. The aggregate model moved
  to Cascade, but the filtered row list is cheap at roughly a thousand rows and
  is tightly coupled to actions (prepare shown, submit prepared, export, bulk
  selection). Rewriting that path in observables would add indirection without a
  measured gain. If the grid grows into the tens of thousands of rows, this is
  the next surface to revisit.
- **Dialog contents.** The raw-log, legend, settings, ask and enrichment dialogs
  are still plain HTML. The context menu is the first overlay; the rest can
  follow the same `overlayFrame` pattern.
- **Themed widgets.** `cascade.ui` is bundled only for the overlay frame. The
  dashboard keeps its own pastel design rather than adopting Cascade's widgets.

## Rebuilding the bundle

The bundle is generated, not hand-edited. From a checkout with node and npm:

```bash
npm install @liquefy/cascade.component @liquefy/cascade.dom @liquefy/cascade.reactive @liquefy/cascade.ui esbuild
npx esbuild entry.js --bundle --format=esm --minify --outfile=tools/web/vendor/cascade.js
```

`entry.js` is the export list recorded in `tools/web/vendor/cascade.NOTICE`.

# Writing the CV: two full pages, no padding
Jobsquirrel · Docs
The generated CV has one job: give a recruiter enough true, specific material to shortlist you in the ten seconds they spend on the first screen. A two-page CV that stops halfway down page two reads as thin even when the facts underneath are strong. This document is the content contract; `cv_target.py` prints the numbers and `check_documents.py` refuses a PDF that fails them. ## The shape | Thing | Target | |---|---| | Pages | exactly 2, both full | | Last page fill | at least 70% (aim for 85-95%) | | Experience bullets | 32-38 in total | | Bullets per role | 6-8 for the two most recent/relevant, 4-6 for the middle, 2-3 for the earliest | | Profile | 150-180 words | | Selected work | 5-6 items | | Skill lines | 7-9 categories | `cv_target.py` prints `CONTENT` (roles, bullets, words, profile length) and `FILL` (page count and how far down each page the text reaches). If either is short, add evidenced detail; never pad. ## The fast, still-grounded path `prepare_role.py` does the deterministic work once: ATS terms, GraphRAG context (reused when the JD hash is unchanged), archetype selection + alignment, and a seed pack copied from the closest existing grounded pack. It writes `state/briefs/.md` with the full JD, grounded context and paths. The model then edits only the parts that should change for the role: profile, tagline, skills, selected work and the role-specific bullet selection/order. The static roles, dates and evidenced achievements are already in the seed, so there is no reason to regenerate them. **A cover letter is the exception, not the rule.** `prepare_role.py` reads the advert and writes `state/letters/.need` (`required:` or `optional:`, with the sentence it based that on). Most adverts do not ask for one. Only when the need says `required` write the letter prose to `state/letters/.json`. `finalise_docs.py` renders the CV with the fill check, renders the letter only if required, gates the exact files (CV only, or CV + letter) with `--record` and (in REVIEW) records PREPARED only on PASS. If an application form turns out to demand a cover letter, rerun `finalise_docs.py --letter-mode yes`. This cuts the slow model's output and the number of turns without skipping any grounding rule or gate. ## No targeting tells - **No job-title line at the top.** The CV opens with the name, contact details and a short capability tagline. The profile does the positioning. An 11pt caps line that repeats the advert's title is the first thing a recruiter sees, and it reads as "this was written for one advert". Leave it out. - The tagline is a capability line ("Backend engineering · real-time distributed systems"), never the job title and never the employer's name. - The letter names the company and role; the CV does not need to. - No JD phrasing copied into the profile or a heading. Mirror the language, do not echo it. ## The bullet formula > **Action + what + how + outcome or scale** (drop the outcome when the evidence > does not support one). Weak (thin, no outcome): > Worked on data pipelines and helped the team deliver projects. Stronger (still true, more specific): > Built a real-time, high-volume caller-fraud detection pipeline on ScyllaDB, > Spring Cloud Data Flow and Prometheus, designed for continuous production load. Strongest (an outcome the record supports): > Delivered a multi-tenant AWS SaaS central hub for distributed SMS gateways at > Google's request, on time and to specification (Keycloak, Spring, Postgres, > React). ## Splitting compound achievements Most thin CVs are thin because each bullet crams two or three separate facts into one line. Split them. This adds length and makes each claim scannable, without inventing anything: Before: > Owned enterprise architecture, strategy, governance and technical direction > across the division, plus the annual budget, headcount plan and technology > roadmap. After (two bullets, same facts): > Owned enterprise architecture, technology strategy, governance and technical > direction across the division. > > Owned the annual budget, headcount plan and technology roadmap, and translated > business strategy into a plan the teams delivered against. Do this with every compound bullet before you consider adding anything new. ## Delivery and team emphasis Hiring managers are not only buying skills; they are buying someone who gets things into production and brings people with them. Every role should carry, where the record supports it: - **One delivery bullet**: what shipped, for whom, to what deadline, at what scale. Use plain verbs: shipped, delivered, launched, rolled out, cut over, handed over, ran in production. - **One team bullet**: who you led or coached, how you set the way of working, how you engaged stakeholders to keep the work moving. - **One operational bullet**, for senior roles: what you owned running, not just building (budget, on-call, reliability, audit). Only write these when the evidence exists. "Delivered on time" is a claim; use it where the record says so (for example a cloud hub at one employer), not as decoration. ## Honesty rules - Use only facts in `config/cv.json`, `config/profile.md` and the role's `state/kb-context/.md`. - Never invent a metric, a team size, a deadline, a tool or an outcome. - Keep the accuracy rules in `config/profile.md`: management scope, titles, certifications and employer descriptions are exact. - If the job asks for something the record does not evidence, leave it out. A gap is better than a claim you have to walk back in the interview. - Product capabilities are not personal achievements; attribute them to the product, and keep your own hands-on work distinct. ## Canonical facts Some facts have one correct wording: an institution's full name, a superlative claim, a product name. `config/canonical-facts.json` holds the exact replacements and the forbidden variants. The knowledge-base ingest applies them before indexing, `cv_target.py` and `render_letter.py` apply them to the content pack before rendering, and `check_documents.py` fails a document that still contains a forbidden variant. Add a rule when a fact must not drift; the public template is `config/canonical-facts.example.json`. ## The loop 1. Write the pack from the KB context, splitting compound bullets and adding the delivery/team bullets the evidence supports. 2. Render: `python3 tools/cv_target.py --key --content state/cv-content/.json --require-fill` 3. If `RESULT: FILL FAIL`, go back to the evidence and add detail. Do not pad, do not shrink the font, do not widen the margins. 4. The pre-submit gate re-measures the PDF and fails a thin CV, so a thin CV cannot be uploaded by accident. ## Why 70% and not 100% A page that ends at 95-100% looks cramped and risks spilling to a third page after a small edit. 85-95% is the sweet spot: full, with room to breathe. Below 70%, the white space at the bottom is the first thing a reader notices. ## No repeated phrases A cover letter must not repeat a phrase of four or more words, and must not repeat the same logistics (notice period, relocation, availability). The pre-submit gate fails on it. `render_letter.py` now checks the `opening` and `fit` prose before rendering and refuses with the exact repeated phrase, so the agent rewrites the sentence instead of producing a document the gate will reject.

# Eligibility and accuracy rules
Jobsquirrel · Docs
The pipeline refuses to apply to roles that don't match your rules, that is a feature, not a limitation. You define the rules in the **Eligibility** and **Accuracy** sections of `config/profile.md`. The runner reads them at the start of every application and records ineligible roles as `CLOSED`/`BLOCKED` with a reason instead of applying. ## 1. Location and work model Say where you are and what you will accept. Example: ``` ## Eligibility - based in: Berlin, Germany - accept: on-site/hybrid in Berlin; fully remote open to Germany and the EU; relocation-supported roles in Switzerland - exclude: on-site roles in other countries; roles requiring fluent ; roles needing local work authorisation you lack - if the location or work model is unclear: do not apply (record BLOCKED) ``` The runner will: apply only if the role fits the `accept` list; record `CLOSED` (no letter, no application) for `exclude` matches; and record `BLOCKED "location unclear"` when it can't tell. Never guess a location to make a role fit. ## 2. Languages List the languages you speak, with honest levels, and the ones you don't: ``` - languages (and honest level): English - native; German - B1 - languages you do NOT speak (never apply to roles that require these): French, Dutch ``` If a role's ad *requires* fluent proficiency in a language you don't speak, the gate closes it. If the location is otherwise fine but the language is merely preferred, the role may still qualify, the runner weighs the wording. ## 3. Stack / technology ("things I don't know") The pipeline will not apply to a role whose primary language/stack you don't use. Put the honest list in `config/profile.md` and keep `config/cv.json`'s languages accurate: ``` ## Accuracy rules (never overstate) - Languages/tech I do NOT use (never apply to a role whose primary stack needs one): Go, C, C++, C#/.NET, Kotlin, Swift, Scala, Ruby, PHP, Elixir, ... - Certifications: list "X (year)" on the certifications list only; never say I "hold" or am "certified in" it; keep it out of the summary. - Management: line management of engineers only (never claim managing managers). - Never claim experience I do not have. ``` `check_alignment.py` enforces this from the **title and the JD body** (so a "Golang" in the tech-stack line or "strong Go experience" in the body is caught even when the title looks generic). Roles that fail are recorded `CLOSED` and skipped, the pipeline must never send you to an interview for something you can't do. ## 4. Accuracy rules (never overstate) These are the claims that must stay true in every generated document: - **Certifications**: list them on the certifications list; do not assert you hold them if you don't, and never say "lapsed". - **Management scope**: say exactly what you managed (e.g. line management of engineers) and nothing more. - **Facts**: every employer, domain, technology and number must already be in `config/cv.json`. `facts.py` fails present-tense claims about past work and flags phrases not supported by the CV; `check_documents.py` blocks unsupported first-person claims. Anything you add here is enforced at generation time (via the runner prompt) and at the pre-submit gate (via `check_documents.py` / `facts.py`). ## 5. Designing your accuracy rules Keep them short, specific and mechanical so they can be enforced: - *Do* name the exact false claims to avoid and the correct alternative. - *Do* state which things go on a list only (certs) vs in prose. - *Don't* encode things the gate can't check (it can't know a metric is right, only whether it's in `cv.json`). When in doubt, leave the claim out and accept lower ATS coverage; a truthful, slightly-less-optimised application beats a fabricated one every time.

# What this is (agent: read this to the user at the start)

*Deliver this to the user when the pipeline is first set up, in your own words,
concise, plain, no jargon. Then ask if they want to proceed with setup.*

---

**In one line:** this is an agent that runs your job search for you, it finds
roles, writes a tailored CV and cover letter for each one, makes sure every claim
is true, applies for you through the employer's own website, and tracks the
replies. You give it your CV and a few rules; it does the repetitive work.
(If you are in the US, "CV" means *resume* throughout, this file included.)

**How it works, end to end**: for each role, in order:

1. **Find**: it watches your inbox (LinkedIn job alerts and recruiter mail) and
   can search job boards, then feeds matching roles into a work queue.
2. **Check eligibility**: it only applies where the role fits your rules (where
   you can work, work authorisation, languages, and the tech you actually use).
   Anything else is recorded as closed, not applied to.
3. **Ground every claim**: it builds a private **knowledge base** from your own
   documents, every version of your CV, project notes, a "brag" doc, talks,
   reviews, a LinkedIn export; **the more you feed it, the better every
   application gets**, and, for each role, pulls out the most relevant, *cited*
   facts. The documents are written only from those facts, so nothing is invented.
4. **Tailor**: it picks the CV family that matches the role, then writes a CV and
   a cover letter targeted at that specific job, in your voice.
5. **Gate**: before anything is sent, it checks the documents for real identity, no
   placeholders, no AI-slop, only supported claims, the right engagement (a
   contract rate only in contract applications), and good keyword coverage
   against the ad. **Nothing is submitted unless it passes.**
6. **Apply**: Camoufox fills in and submits the employer's own
   application (Teamtailor, Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workday, …), answering
   questions honestly from your rules.
7. **Record**: it stores exactly what was sent (the files, their hashes and a
   snapshot) and updates a single register: one row per company + role.
8. **Track replies**: it reads your inbox to mark interviews, rejections and
   confirmations, and surfaces any email-verification links for you to click.

**The two things it will never do wrong on purpose:** it never fabricates, and it
never sends a document that fails the gate. If a job wants something your CV
can't evidence, it leaves it out.

**Be clear about the boundaries:** this is **not** a fully-automatic bot. It
follows a written set of instructions (and works best with a capable model), and
it needs you for the calls only you can make, your rules, approving any email
before it goes, and solving a CAPTCHA/2FA when a site demands it. Think "a
tireless assistant working under your instructions", not "press go and forget it".

**Ways you can run it** (I'll explain and you choose):

- **Discover**: just find new roles and add them to the queue.
- **Review / Prepare**: build the tailored CVs and letters and let **you review
  them before anything is sent**. Nothing goes out.
- **Apply**: full auto. Build the documents, gate them, and submit. (This is the
  default; it applies to the most senior roles first.)
- **Apply with a fixed CV**: use one CV for everything (fast, less tailored).
- **One role at a time**: for a single job or a retry.

**What I'll need from you:**

- Some details about you, your rules, and the claims you must never overstate
  (I'll interview you, you won't fill in forms).
- Your CV and **as much other material as you can share**: every old CV, a
  project/brag doc, design notes, talks, reviews (this is what makes the
  knowledge base, and therefore every application, sharp and specific).
- Optional: access so I can track replies, read-only Gmail, and a one-time
  LinkedIn login for manual use. The public build does not automate Easy Apply.
- A few human-only moments as they come up: solving a CAPTCHA/2FA, and approving
  any email before it's sent.

**Your privacy and control:**

- Gmail is **read-only** by default (single scope); the pipeline can't send,
  change or delete your mail. Sending is a separate tool that needs your explicit
  approval of the recipient, subject and content, every time. Deleting mail is a
  gated tool that needs explicit per-use authorisation, you'll likely never use it.
- Secrets and tokens live **outside** the project folder; your CV, rules and
  applications stay git-ignored.
- Everything is recorded, so you can always see what was sent to whom, and when. There is a local
  **web dashboard** (single grid of every application, a live run view, the knowledge graph and the
  agent chat) if you like to watch or configure things directly.

**What happens next:** I'll install what I need, interview you, write your
configuration, build your CV templates, build the knowledge base, and set up your
accounts, then show you the run modes and start finding roles.

Shall we begin?

# Knowledge base (GraphRAG)
Jobsquirrel · Docs
The knowledge base is the retrieval layer that keeps generated documents **truthful**. It is a Microsoft [GraphRAG](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/) index over your own documents. `tools/kb_graphrag.py` is the single retrieval path: given a job description it returns a **cited context pack** of your most relevant achievements, skills, metrics and certifications, which the agent then uses as the only source of claims. It is **required**: the agent builds a targeted CV and cover letter for each role **from the cited context pack** this produces. (Grounding can fall back to `config/cv.json` only if you truly cannot run GraphRAG, but targeted document generation depends on it.) ## How it fits the pipeline ``` kb/sources/*.txt --graphrag index--> kb/graphrag/output/ (graph + vectors) │ a job description --tools/kb_graphrag.py--> state/kb-context/.md (cited pack) │ agent writes CV/letter ONLY from this pack + config/cv.json ``` `tools/kb_graphrag.py --jd --out state/kb-context/.md` runs a GraphRAG local search (`--method local|global|drift`) and writes the pack. `--check` verifies the index and the embeddings backend are up. ## 1. Curate sources: the more, the better The knowledge base is only as rich as the corpus you feed it. **Do not stop at your CV.** Dump everything truthful and specific you have into `kb/sources/`, a larger corpus directly produces sharper, more targeted, more honest documents, because retrieval can find the *exact right* fact for each ad, **with a citation**. Put your documents there, **any format** (PDF, DOCX, DOC/ODT, HTML, Markdown, email, CSV/JSON). You can drop them into `kb/sources/` by hand, or **upload them from the web UI** (**Settings → Knowledge base**, then *Rebuild graph*) and see exactly what the index contains under **Settings → GraphRAG**. - **Every version of your CV**: a master plus each old/role-specific one. Different versions hold different bullets; the graph merges them. - **A "brag document"**: every project with numbers such as scale, users, revenue, latency, uptime, team sizes, budgets, outcomes. - **Project / design / architecture notes**, RFCs, postmortems, talks, blog and README excerpts. - **Performance reviews / feedback**, awards, publications. - **Your LinkedIn export** (positions, skills, recommendations, certifications). - **Anything else truthful** that evidences what you've done. Rules: - Keep **every fact traceable to a real experience**: this corpus is the ground truth the gate checks against. - Prefer **specifics** (numbers, technologies, scope) over adjectives. - **Any format works.** The ingest step below converts PDF/DOCX/DOC/ODT/HTML/ email/Markdown to text (and passes `.txt`/`.csv`/`.json` straight through), so there is nothing to convert by hand. Then ingest them (any format → GraphRAG text input): ```bash python3 tools/kb_ingest.py --sources kb/sources --out kb/graphrag/input ``` ## 2. Configure models Copy and edit: ```bash cp kb/graphrag/settings.example.yaml kb/graphrag/settings.yaml cp kb/graphrag/.env.example kb/graphrag/.env ``` - **Completion model**: any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`GRAPHRAG_API_BASE`, `GRAPHRAG_API_KEY`, `GRAPHRAG_LLM_MODEL`): including a **local** llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM server. The graph builder then runs entirely on your machine. - **Embeddings**: any OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint (`GRAPHRAG_EMBED_BASE`, `GRAPHRAG_EMBED_MODEL`, `GRAPHRAG_EMBED_KEY`). ### Embeddings backend and acceleration Embeddings run locally, so this is the one part worth accelerating. `tools/embeddings.sh` starts a `llama.cpp` (`llama-server`) with the embedding model (`nomic-embed-text` by default) behind an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings` on `127.0.0.1:11435`, and **auto-selects the best backend**: | Your machine | Backend (auto) | llama.cpp build to install | | --- | --- | --- | | Apple Silicon (macOS) | `metal` | `brew install llama.cpp` (Metal is built in) | | NVIDIA GPU (Linux/Windows) | `cuda` | a CUDA build (`-DGGML_CUDA=ON`) or a prebuilt CUDA release | | AMD / Intel GPU | `vulkan` | a Vulkan build (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`) or a prebuilt Vulkan release | | No GPU | `cpu` | any build | ```bash bash tools/embeddings.sh --check # report server, model, backend, endpoint bash tools/embeddings.sh # start it (idempotent) EMBED_BACKEND=cuda bash tools/embeddings.sh # force a backend: metal|cuda|vulkan|cpu ``` Notes: - `EMBED_NGL` (default `99`) is how many layers to offload to the GPU; `99` means all of them. `LLAMA_SERVER` is the path to `llama-server` (or the directory holding it), `EMBED_MODEL` the `.gguf`, `EMBED_PORT` the port. - If your `llama-server` binary was not built with the selected backend, it will fall back to CPU. Check the log (`EMBED_LOG`, default `/tmp/llama-server.log`) for the `offloaded N/N layers to GPU` line to confirm acceleration is active. - Any other OpenAI-compatible embeddings server works too. Point `GRAPHRAG_EMBED_BASE` at it and ignore `embeddings.sh`. > **Small-context embeddings:** if your embedding model has a small context (e.g. > 2048 tokens), keep `community_reports.max_length` modest (the template uses > 1000) so every community report fits and embeds without error. ## 3. Build the index ```bash bash tools/embeddings.sh # ensure the backend is up (auto backend) pip install graphrag # or use .venv-graphrag python3 -m graphrag index --root kb/graphrag # one-off; can take many minutes python3 tools/kb_graphrag.py --check # index + backend + CLI ``` Indexing calls the LLM to extract entities/relationships and summarise communities; it costs tokens and time. It caches completed steps, so a re-run after a failure resumes rather than restarting. ### Canonical facts Before indexing, `kb_ingest.py` applies `config/canonical-facts.json` to every source, so the graph cannot learn a wrong variant of a fact that has one correct wording. The same rules are applied when a CV or letter is rendered, and the pre-submit gate fails a document that still contains a forbidden variant. The public template is `config/canonical-facts.example.json`. ## 4. Use it ```bash python3 tools/kb_graphrag.py --jd state/job-descriptions/.md \ --out state/kb-context/.md python3 tools/kb_graphrag.py --method drift --jd ... # deeper pass (slower) ``` The runner does this automatically (step "grounding") for each queued role. ## 4b. The Knowledge workspace The dashboard's top-bar **Knowledge** page is a full-page, interactive view of the index. It is deliberately more than a graph picture: - **Universe**: every entity, grouped into level-0 themes as islands, with weighted importance, zoom-tiered labels, community nebulae and a focus control. - **Map**: the same renderer drilled down through **Topics** (ontology classes), **Communities** (the generated hierarchy), **Entities** and **Ego** networks. - **Focus**: selecting an entity frames its neighbourhood, lights the selected node and its hops, dims the rest, then fades back after a few seconds. Clicking empty space restores the previous view and the normal labels. - **Node pane**: description, class, sources, neighbours, strongest connections, subgraph depth and layer counts. Descriptions and types can be edited and evidence-backed links added; changes live in overlays, not the generated index. - **Ask**: cited answers from the graph in local, global, basic and drift modes. - **Semantic search**: entity search by meaning, not exact wording. - **Role evidence**: job-ad keywords mapped to grounded entities and explicit gaps. - **Grounded enrichment**: reviewable additions supported by existing text; approved nodes and links are gold and marked as grounded. - **Sources / Add / Roles**: upload and rebuild the corpus, record a fact or skill without a rebuild, and open a role in the application drawer. The full guide, including controls, the orphan policy, the quality gate and the maintenance workflow, is **[KNOWLEDGE-GRAPH.md](KNOWLEDGE-GRAPH.md)**. ## 5. Maintain it - When you add or change a source, copy it into `kb/graphrag/input/` and **re-index** (`graphrag index --root kb/graphrag`). Stale indexes surface stale claims. - **Accuracy first:** if a source once contained an overstatement, fixing the source and re-indexing is what stops it reappearing in generated documents. - Keep secrets out: `kb/graphrag/.env` and `settings.yaml` are git-ignored. ## Troubleshooting | Symptom | Fix | |---|---| | `embeddings backend DOWN` | `bash tools/embeddings.sh`; check `EMBED_PORT` and the log. | | `input (...) is larger than the max context size` | Lower `community_reports.max_length`; re-index. | | GraphRAG CLI missing | `pip install graphrag` (or set `GRAPHRAG_BIN`). | | Every run re-computes | Ensure `cache.type: json` persists between runs. | ## 6. Employment-contract material is excluded The graph is for work evidence, not the legal machinery of a contract. Contract and legal documents are excluded at ingest (`kb/sources/.ingestignore` includes `contracts/*`, `reference-cv/*Contract*` and `reference-cv/*Juridiska*`). `tools/graph_prune_sensitive.py` removes any contract/legal entities that slipped through: garden leave, pay in lieu of notice, notice/probation, disciplinary/grievance terms, salary/bonus/pension details, courts, tribunals, jurisdiction and generic contract parties. It also removes any entity left with no surviving text unit, its relationships, ungrounded communities and reports, recomputes degrees, drops dangling edges, cleans orphan vector rows and redacts surviving descriptions and community reports. `tools/sensitive.py` redacts context packs and query answers as a backstop. Every entity should also have at least one relationship. Curated, evidence-backed links for missed entities live in `kb/graphrag/orphan-links.json` and are applied with `tools/graph_attach_orphans.py`; the Universe keeps any genuinely unlinked entity in a labelled **Unlinked evidence** island. Run the gate after a rebuild or prune: ```bash .venv-graphrag/bin/python tools/graph_quality.py --fail-sensitive --fail-orphans ``` The `sensitive` line must stay at zero, `grounding` must show no entity without a text unit, and `orphans` must show zero. See **[KNOWLEDGE-GRAPH.md](KNOWLEDGE-GRAPH.md)** for the full workflow.

# The knowledge graph workspace
Jobsquirrel · Docs
The **Knowledge** page is the visual layer over the GraphRAG index. It is not a picture of the index: it is a working surface for inspecting evidence, finding gaps, asking questions, and making grounded additions without editing the generated index by hand. The screenshots below use a small **synthetic demo graph** (fictional people, companies and projects), so the documentation can be public without exposing a real job search. Your own graph looks denser because it has your own evidence. | The Universe: themes as islands, weighted stars and a focus ring | Focus: the selected entity, its neighbourhood and the details pane | |---|---| | ![The knowledge universe: eight synthetic theme islands connected by a central person](screenshots/graph-universe.png) | ![A selected synthetic person with the node details pane and bright neighbouring clusters](screenshots/graph-focus.png) | | Map: the generated community hierarchy | |---| | ![The Map view showing eight synthetic communities](screenshots/graph-communities.png) | ## 1. What the graph is made of The graph is built from `kb/sources/` by Microsoft GraphRAG into `kb/graphrag/output/`: | Table | What it holds | |---|---| | `entities.parquet` | Every person, organisation, role, skill, technology, project, metric, team, certification and concept, with a description, degree and source text units. | | `relationships.parquet` | The evidence-backed links between entities, with a description, weight and source text units. | | `communities.parquet` | The generated hierarchy (level 0 themes, then sub-communities) and the entities in each. | | `community_reports.parquet` | The generated summary, findings and rating for each community. | | `documents.parquet` / `text_units.parquet` | The source documents and the passages every claim is traced to. | Two operator overlays sit beside the index and are merged at read time: - `kb/graphrag/enrichment.json`: approved entities and links. New links are drawn in gold and marked as grounded. - `kb/graphrag/edits.json`: description and type overrides for existing nodes. `kb/graphrag/orphan-links.json` holds the curated links used to attach entities that GraphRAG extracted without a relationship. See §9. The overlay survives a rebuild. The generated tables do not; a rebuild replaces them, and the overlays are applied again on top. ## 2. Two renderers, five ways to look **Universe** is the whole graph. Every level-0 community is an island; the best-connected entity gives the island its name. It is for orientation: where the themes are, which entities carry them, and how the evidence crosses from one theme to another. **Map** is the drill-down renderer. It starts at the ontology or the community hierarchy, then opens into the entities behind a class or community. It uses the same point-star renderer, colours, importance, focus and fade as the Universe, but on a subset. | View | What it shows | How to open it | |---|---|---| | **Topics** | Ontology classes (Person, Organisation, Role, Skill, Technology, Project, Metric, Certification, Team, Platform, Product, Concept) with counts and the aggregated links between classes. | Knowledge → Map → **Topics**, or the **Topics** chip on the Universe. | | **Communities** | The generated community hierarchy; double-click a community to descend until you reach entities. | Knowledge → Map → **Communities**. | | **Entities** | The entities behind a topic or a leaf community. | Click a topic or open a community. | | **Ego** | One entity plus its direct neighbours. | Double-click an entity, or **Focus ego network** in the node pane. | | **Universe** | Every entity, grouped into level-0 theme islands. | **Knowledge** → the **Universe** toggle. | Search works in every view. **Semantic** runs a natural-language search over the entity vector store; results show similarity, impact and type, and selecting one opens the same node pane. ## 3. Moving around | Action | Result | |---|---| | Drag | Orbit the camera. | | Wheel / trackpad | Zoom toward the point under the cursor. | | Right-drag or Shift-drag | Pan. | | `W A S D` | Fly through the scene; `Q` / `E` move down / up. | | `Shift` | Boost the fly speed. | | Click a star | Select the entity and open its details. | | Double-click a star | Open its ego network in the Map. | | Click an island label | Travel to that theme. | | `Esc` | Leave the Universe and return to the Map. | | Click empty space | Clear the focus and return to the previous view. | | **Reset view** | Return to the overview camera. | Text selection is disabled across the graph and its labels, so dragging never leaves a blue highlight behind. Form fields in the side pane remain selectable. ## 4. Focus, the timed fade and labels Selecting an entity does three things: 1. **It frames the neighbourhood.** The camera centres the entity and pulls back far enough to include its direct neighbours. An entity attached from the overlay (a skill linked to a person, for example) frames its anchor instead. 2. **It lights the subgraph.** The selected node and its neighbours keep their colour, gain a stronger halo and grow; everything outside the focus drops to near black. Level of detail no longer hides a neighbour that lives in another island. 3. **It labels the neighbourhood.** The selected node and its direct neighbours are labelled even when the zoomed label range would normally drop them. The dimming is **temporary**. It holds for about four seconds and then fades back over roughly one second. The selected node keeps its marker, size and label, so you never lose what you selected. Clicking empty space clears the selection, restores the view that was active before it, and re-runs the normal label assignment immediately. The **Focus** control sets how many hops stay bright: - Universe: a slider (1-3 hops, default 2) in the bottom HUD. - Map: a selector in the toolbar (1-3 hops, default 1). Outside a focus, labels are tiered by zoom: the overview shows the key node of each large island and the top hubs; zooming in reveals well-connected entities, then named entities, then local detail. **Label reach** (Universe HUD) bounds how far from the camera labels are drawn; it tightens automatically as you zoom in. ## 5. Weighted importance Not every entity is equally important. `tools/graph_importance.py` runs a small weighted message-passing pass over the relationship graph and scores each entity from its connections, relationship weights, type and impact language in the description. The degree of an entity matters, but a well-evidenced project or a landmark outcome can outrank a merely well-connected name. Those scores drive: - node size and label priority; - the order of topics and highlights in retrieval; - the **impact** percentage in the node pane; - which entities surface first in search and role evidence. The cache is `state/graph-importance.json`; it is regenerated when the index changes. High-impact nodes are the warm glow you see above the long tail. ## 6. The node pane Clicking a star opens the details pane. It is the source of truth for what the node is and why it is in the graph: - title, ontology class, degree, mentions and community; - description and, when available, an evidence note; - **Subgraph**: node/link counts, maximum depth and a layer-by-layer breakdown; - **Sources**: the documents behind the entity, clickable in the Sources tab; - **Neighbours**: every directly connected entity, sorted by degree; - **Strongest connections**: the highest-weight local relationships; - **Edit details**: override the description or ontology type; the change goes to `edits.json`, not the generated index; - **Add connection**: create a grounded link to another entity with the evidence that supports it; the link goes to `enrichment.json`; - **Focus ego network**: open the entity and its neighbours in the Map; - **Open community**: travel to the community that contains it. Overridden types and descriptions are visible everywhere the node appears, including search and context packs. ## 7. Ask the graph **Ask** turns a natural-language question into a cited answer from the index. It is not a chat model guessing from the CV; it is the graph retrieval engine: - **Local**: follows the entities and relationships nearest the question. - **Global**: uses community reports for a theme-level answer. - **Basic**: a direct vector retrieval pass. - **Drift**: a deeper local pass that follows several neighbourhoods. Every answer carries citations to the source documents and entities. Use it to answer questions such as "where is the evidence for the fraud platform?" or "which roles show identity and access management?" before writing a CV line. If the graph cannot support an answer, the answer says so instead of inventing one. ## 8. Role evidence, semantic search and enrichment **Role evidence** maps the saved job ad's keywords to entities in the graph and shows two lists: what the evidence supports and what it cannot confirm. That distinction is what keeps generated CVs honest. A missing keyword is a gap to leave out or address in the letter, not a claim to invent. **Semantic search** searches the entity descriptions by meaning, not by exact word. It is useful when the ad uses different language from your documents ("identity federation" versus "SSO/SAML"). **Grounded enrichment** proposes additions that are supported by existing text: a technology mentioned but not linked, a certification that is in the sources, a high-impact relationship, or an unrepresented metric. Every proposal is shown for review with its evidence. Approved nodes and links are marked as grounded and rendered in gold. Nothing is added silently. ## 9. No orphans: attaching unlinked evidence An entity with no relationships cannot support a claim and has no place in a theme. The graph therefore aims for **zero orphans**. There are three layers: 1. **GraphRAG extraction** normally produces relationships for every entity. 2. **The operator overlay** can attach a missed entity to the entities it obviously belongs with. The curated mapping lives in `kb/graphrag/orphan-links.json`; each entry names a target, a short description and the evidence it rests on. 3. **`tools/graph_attach_orphans.py`** applies the mapping: ```bash python3 tools/graph_attach_orphans.py --report python3 tools/graph_attach_orphans.py --apply ``` It writes links to `enrichment.json`, places the attached entity in the level-0 community of its first mapped target, and refuses to write while any orphan is still unmapped. The link is a **display and retrieval aid**, not a new biographical claim: the description and evidence must come from the entity's own source text. If an entity is genuinely unlinked and no honest link exists, the Universe keeps it in a grey **Unlinked evidence** island rather than scattering it as a stray star. The node pane explains that no relationship was extracted. The quality gate reports it until it is either linked with evidence or removed. ## 10. Context packs and hybrid retrieval The same graph produces the cited pack that grounds each CV and letter. The pack is not a dump of the whole index: - it starts from the job description and selects the relevant entities and relationships; - **leadership-oriented roles** add global career themes and a coarser community level, while technical roles stay precise; - weighted highlights, operator edits and approved links are appended so a landmark fact is not lost in a local search; - only facts with a source are included; - contract and legal material is redacted before the pack is written. `tools/kb_graphrag.py` is the single retrieval path. The pack is saved as `state/kb-context/.md` and is the only evidence the document writer may use. ## 11. Privacy: contract and legal material never enters The graph is for work evidence, not the legal machinery of an employment contract. This is enforced at several points: - `kb/sources/.ingestignore` excludes `contracts/*`, `reference-cv/*Contract*` and `reference-cv/*Juridiska*` before indexing. - `tools/sensitive.py` holds the blocked title terms and the redaction terms (notice, probation, garden leave, salary, court, tribunal, jurisdiction, severance, settlement and similar), and strips personal identifiers such as email addresses and national identity numbers. - `tools/graph_prune_sensitive.py` removes blocked entities, entities left with no surviving text unit, their relationships, ungrounded communities and their reports; it recomputes degrees, drops dangling edges, redacts surviving descriptions/reports and cleans orphan vector rows. - A git-ignored `kb/graphrag/private-redactions.txt` can add a locality, a former name or another private term without putting it in public code; the loader appends those terms to the redaction list at runtime. - Context packs and Ask answers are redacted as a backstop. - The quality gate fails if any blocked title, sensitive description, sensitive report or ungrounded entity remains. The rule is simple: **if a fact exists only in a contract or legal document, it is not in the graph.** ## 12. Quality gate Run this after a rebuild or a prune: ```bash .venv-graphrag/bin/python tools/graph_quality.py --fail-sensitive --fail-orphans ``` It reports: - entity, relationship, text-unit and community counts; - the degree distribution, including the long tail; - exact and near-duplicate titles; - teams in the wrong ontology class; - community levels and the largest communities; - relationship self-loops and duplicate pairs; - sensitive titles, descriptions and reports; - entities with no surviving text unit; - entities with no link after overlays (orphans). The command exits non-zero on sensitive/ungrounded material (`--fail-sensitive`) or on any orphan (`--fail-orphans`). A healthy graph prints zero on all three: no sensitive titles, no ungrounded entities, no orphans. ## 13. Maintaining the graph ```bash bash tools/setup_kb.sh # ingest, embed, index .venv-graphrag/bin/python tools/graph_prune_sensitive.py --apply python3 tools/graph_attach_orphans.py --apply .venv-graphrag/bin/python tools/graph_quality.py --fail-sensitive --fail-orphans ``` - **Incremental indexing is not reliable** with the current GraphRAG pipeline. The reliable path is a full rebuild, then prune, then attach. - **Overlays survive rebuilds**; the generated parquet tables do not. Re-run the prune and the orphan attachment after every rebuild. - **Adding a document** requires a rebuild. **Adding a skill or fact** from the dashboard does not: it is appended to every context pack immediately and shown through the live skill overlay, so you can re-prepare a role without waiting for an index. - **Stale indexes are dangerous**: they surface stale claims. If a source was wrong, fix the source and rebuild; do not edit the generated pack by hand. ## 14. Limits worth knowing - The Universe is a summary. A community with hundreds of entities is drawn as a dense island; the Map and the node pane are for detail. - Community reports are generated at index time. After a prune, an affected report may be removed until the next rebuild; the entities and links are still current. - Overlay links are keyed by entity title. Renaming an entity in a rebuilt index can orphan an overlay link; the quality gate will show the orphan. - A very small graph looks sparse in the Universe: the layout is designed for hundreds to thousands of entities. Use the Map for small graphs. - The 3D scene needs WebGL. Without it, the page shows a readable fallback and the rest of the dashboard still works. ## Duplicates GraphRAG can extract the same thing twice, or split an employer into its legal entities ("Acme", "Acme UK Ltd", "Acme Singapore Pte Ltd"). After a rebuild, run: ```bash python3 tools/graph_dedupe.py # list the merges python3 tools/graph_dedupe.py --apply # merge them in the index ``` It merges titles that normalise to the same string within a type, and organisation variants that reduce to an existing organisation once legal suffixes (Ltd, Pte Ltd, AB, ...) and office qualifiers (UK, Singapore, APAC, HQ, ...) are stripped. Aliases are recorded in the surviving entity, text units are unioned, relationships are rewritten and duplicate edges summed. Symbols such as C, C# and C++ are never merged. A timestamped backup is written under `state/backups/` first. ## Typed relations and per-role weighting GraphRAG types entities but leaves every edge as an undifferentiated relationship. `tools/graph_relations.py --apply` classifies each edge with the ontology vocabulary (`HELD_ROLE`, `AT_ORGANIZATION`, `USES`, `DELIVERED`, `EVIDENCED_BY`, `CERTIFIED_IN`, `STUDIED_AT`, `SPEAKS`, `RELATED_TO`) from its endpoints' classes and its description, and writes a `relation_type` column. `tools/setup_kb.sh` runs it after every index. `tools/ontology.py` also carries **profiles**: a per-class weighting for each kind of role (leadership, ai, data, security, architecture). The playground picks a profile from the role text and uses it to rank seeds and order the traversal, so the same graph produces a leadership-shaped CV for one role and a technology-shaped one for another. The payload reports the profile and weights it used, and the build rail shows them.

Status: living document · Owner: repo owner · Applies to this repository. --- ## 1. Purpose Jobsquirrel is an open, self-hosted, **agent-driven job-application pipeline**. The human supplies a CV and a set of rules; an AI coding agent then discovers roles, tailors a CV per role (a cover letter only when the advert asks for one), gates them for accuracy and quality, submits applications through a real browser, tracks replies from the inbox, and keeps a single source of truth for every application and the exact files sent. **Principles (non-negotiable):** | Principle | Meaning | |---|---| | Honest | Never fabricate. Claims must be backed by the knowledge base + config. | | Gated | Nothing is submitted until the alignment + pre-submit gates PASS. | | Auditable | Every submission records the exact bytes (hash + snapshot) and the evidence. | | Agent-agnostic | Drives opencode, Claude Code, `hermes`, `pi`, or any CLI agent. | | Dependency-light | CLI tools are stdlib/plain; no framework, no build step. | | Human-in-control | Irreversible actions (send/delete email, apply) require approval. | | Person/country-agnostic | Everything personal lives in `config/`, never in code. | ## 2. Personas & roles - **Candidate**: the owner. Supplies CV/rules, reviews output, approves risky actions, solves CAPTCHA/2FA. - **Agent**: an AI coding agent that operates the repo via its CLI tools (contract: `AGENTS.md`). - **Human-assist**: the person completing steps the automation must not (CAPTCHA, final submit in their own browser). ## 3. Architecture ``` discover -> queue -> per-role: JD + keywords + GraphRAG context -> tailored CV + letter -> alignment gate + pre-submit gate -> submit via browser (Camoufox) -> record (hash + snapshot) -> reconcile replies (Gmail, read-only) -> outcomes + dashboard ``` Components: - **CLI tools** (`tools/*.py`, `tools/*.sh`): one concern each; the contract for the agent. - **Agent harness** (`tools/agent_run.sh`, `tools/run_queue.sh`): resolves the agent and runs one headless task per role. - **Browser** (`tools/camoufox_server.py` + `camoufox_browser.py`): Camoufox browser for real ATS forms. - **Knowledge base**: GraphRAG over `kb/sources/` (grounding for generated documents). - **State**: plain files under `state/` (the source of truth). - **Dashboard** (`tools/dashboard.py`): web UI (this spec, §9). ## 4. Data model (files are the API) | Path | Contents | |---|---| | `state/applications.csv` | Canonical register: `date,company,role,ats,status,letter,notes,employment,action,key,apply_url`. Status model `QUEUED | SUBMITTED | IN_PROGRESS | INTERVIEW | OFFER | REJECTED | BLOCKED | MANUAL | PREPARED | CLOSED`. - **Follow-up flags** (`action` in the register; a flag in the grid, a toolbar filter, and editable in the row drawer). Set explicitly on the row; otherwise guessed from the saved job ad, then the notes; `unknown` when nothing says. - `INTERVIEW` is one stored status with three display labels, derived from the row's notes (the status itself never changes): **`SCHEDULED`** when the notes contain a future interview date, **`INVITED`** when they only show an invitation or an availability exchange ("invited", "book", "availability", "reschedule"), and plain **`INTERVIEW`** otherwise. Safety & approval model 1. **Accuracy gates.** Nothing is uploaded until `check_alignment` and `check_documents` both PASS; `--record` writes a **hash-stamped receipt**, and `record_submission.py` refuses to record `SUBMITTED` without a matching receipt for the exact files. 2. **Evidence.** A `SUBMITTED` row needs the real confirmation text/URL; placeholders are refused. Missing receipt/evidence ⇒ recorded as `forced` (marked `[forced]`). 3. **Approval gate (`approval.py`).** Irreversible actions require explicit approval: - interactive: `Approve …? [y/N]` (only on a TTY), or - non-interactive: `APPROVE_=1` for that one command. Every decision (granted/refused) is appended to `state/approvals.log`. Default is **ask-or-refuse, never silent**. 4. **CAPTCHA/2FA.** Stop, record `BLOCKED`, never evade. 5. **Email.** Draft-first: the agent saves a reply (`draft_email.py`), the human presses **Send with approval** in the drawer, edits the exact email in the approval dialog if needed, and only then does `gmail_send.py` send that draft (one-time receipt; no env bypass). Mailbox deletion uses a separate `gmail.modify` token and `gmail_delete.py --authorize AUTHORIZE-DELETE`. 6. **Web UI.** Binds `127.0.0.1`; every write needs a per-session token (anti-CSRF); risky actions also gated (see §9). 7. **Recruitment-scam checks (`tools/scam_check.py`).** Every saved advert and every scanned message is checked for the known scam families: remote-access software (AnyDesk/TeamViewer/RustDesk), wallet/seed-phrase requests, pay-to-work fees, equipment cheques, task scams, money mules, reshipping, crypto salaries, labour-trafficking red flags, recovery scams, chat-only interviews, unrealistic pay, early ID/bank details, pressure and free-mailbox senders. A **HIGH** signal blocks `prepare_role.py` (exit 3; `--allow-scam` overrides after human verification), and the signal is stored in `state/scam/.json`, shown as a scam marker on the grid and a red/amber banner in the role drawer and the Gmail review. The hard rule: never download or install software for an interview, never join a chat-only interview, never share a wallet/seed phrase/private key, never pay a fee or move money. See `docs/SCAMS.md`. Mail is checked against the company's apply domain (lookalikes), free mailboxes, Reply-To mismatches, links (installers, IP/punycode hosts, wallet-connect, file hosts) and attachments (executables, archives); the worst warning per role is kept in `state/scam-emails.json`. Roles with a HIGH or specific MEDIUM signal are grouped in the **Probably scams** bucket, separate from **Needs you**. ## 8. Repository model One repository, self-contained. # Releases
Jobsquirrel · Docs
## Privacy (release notes are public) Release titles, notes, tags, commit messages and the code are all public. **Never** put the candidate's personal data or live pipeline state in them. In particular, never write: - the candidate's name, email, phone, LinkedIn/website, city/country or pay target; - a specific country, city, currency code or market name; - employers, recruiters, job titles or companies from the live register; - real counts from the register ("22 need you", "441 ongoing"), interview dates or mailbox/application statistics. Describe features generically: "a role", "the candidate", "a configurable pay floor", "a company name mentioned in passing". Use synthetic examples (`Acme`, `ExampleCorp`). Screenshots, logs and examples must be redacted or synthetic. If in doubt, leave it out. ## Versioning - `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. Cut a release when a coherent feature set lands, not for every fix. Until the project has users, keep the history to milestones: one release per minor line, plus a patch only when a milestone needs a fix before the next minor. - Bump the `VERSION` file to match; the in-app **update check** compares it to the latest GitHub release. ## Naming - **Release titles must be funny AND squirrel-adjacent.** The well is where a squirrel lives and what it lives in: dens, dreys, lodges, setts, holts, warrens and nests, or tree types (oak, ash, elm, beech, yew, cedar, pine, spruce, larch, willow, holm). - Rotation: **patch releases (0.5.x) use den/nest words; minor releases (0.6+) use tree types.** A mixed pun is fine when it earns the laugh. - Patch examples: *"Nest Practice"*, *"Den and Dusted"*, *"Lair Necessities"*, *"Warren Peace"*, *"Sett For Life"*, *"Drey Area"*, *"Holt On"*. - Minor examples: *"Cedar Than Never"*, *"Fir Real"*, *"Spruce Springsteen"*, *"Elm Street"*, *"The Holm Truth"*, *"Larch-itecture"*, *"Poplar Opinion"*. - It must actually be a joke: a plain phrase ("Room to Grow") does not qualify, and a funny name with no squirrel/tree angle does not either. Rename it before publishing. - Title format: `vX.Y.Z "Funny Title"` (one emoji is fine). The GitHub release title can be reworded after publication without moving the tag. ## Cutting one ```bash # 0. write the notes to /tmp/notes.md, then lint them (must print RESULT: PASS) python3 tools/release_lint.py --text-file /tmp/notes.md # 0b. scan the repo for live credentials (must print RESULT: PASS) python3 tools/secret_scan.py # 1. bump the version printf 'X.Y.Z\n' > VERSION # 2. commit and push, then tag (annotated) and push the tag git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m 'vX.Y.Z "Funny Title"' && git push origin vX.Y.Z # 3. create the GitHub Release with the same name and notes (via the API; gh isn't required) ``` Never publish notes that fail `release_lint.py`. The release notes follow the house voice: a one-line gag, a theme sentence, then **What we dragged into the drey** (bullets) and, when relevant, a **Loose bark** section for behaviour that changed. (Earlier releases used "The nuts we added" / "Cracked shells"; leave them as they are.) `secret_scan.py` checks tracked/untracked files and git history for live key formats and for the exact values in the private agent/GraphRAG config. It never prints a secret. A hit in history is still a leak: rotate the key and purge the history; deleting it from the tip is not enough.

# Run modes
Jobsquirrel · Docs
The pipeline can be run several ways. **The agent should explain these to the user and let them choose**, the user should never have to read this file. ## Run completion Every finished queue appends a summary of each task's outcome to the **Agent** pane (and `state/logs/run-complete.log`). A detached run no longer disappears silently when its badge clears: you see what was prepared, submitted, blocked or closed, with the reason. ## 1. Discover (find roles, no applications) Find new roles and feed the queue; generate nothing. ```bash python3 tools/discover.py # from LinkedIn Job Alert emails (dry run) python3 tools/discover.py --queue # add new matches to state/queue.tsv python3 tools/email_opportunities.py --apply # recruiter/contract leads -> register python3 tools/prioritise_queue.py # order the queue most-senior-first ``` ## 2. Review / Prepare (generate documents, do NOT send) For every queued role: build the **grounded, targeted CV and cover letter**, run the alignment and pre-submit gates, save the files, and record the row as `PREPARED`. **Nothing is submitted.** Use this to review documents before sending. ```bash REVIEW=1 PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh ``` Outputs per role: `state/kb-context/.md`, `state/cv-content/.json`, `documents/applications/_CV_.docx` (+ `.pdf`) and `documents/applications/_Motivation_.docx`. Review them, then move the roles you're happy with to an apply run (or send them yourself). ## 3. Apply (generated, role-targeted CVs), the default Full end-to-end: build the targeted documents, gate them, submit through the employer's ATS, and record provenance. ```bash PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh ``` Each queued role's CV is **generated for that role** (aligned to its family and grounded in the knowledge base). This is the highest-quality mode. ## 4. Apply with a fixed CV (no per-role generation) Use **one** CV for every role in the run, no grounding, no per-role CV/letter. Fast and cheap (e.g. a "general" CV), lower targeting. ```bash LIGHT=1 FIXED_CV=documents/archetypes/_CV_.docx \ PARALLEL=3 bash tools/run_queue.sh ``` The runner still does the eligibility/duplicate gates and records the outcome. Before any task starts it runs the pre-submit gate once on the fixed CV (`check_documents.py --cv --record`: your name, no template leftovers, no present-tense claims about past employers, no contract rate in a full-time run). If the CV fails, the run stops with the reasons and nothing is sent; if it passes, the receipt lets every submission be recorded without `--force`. ## 5. One role at a time (manual, for control or a retry) Drive the per-role steps directly (see `AGENTS.md` §4): save the ad, extract ATS keywords, ground with GraphRAG, pick the aligned archetype, build the targeted CV + letter, gate, apply, record. Ideal for a single URL or a re-run. ## Choosing the CV per role - The queue's 4th column is the **starting archetype** (e.g. leadership vs AI-platform vs security); the runner verifies alignment and switches if needed. - **Generated** CVs (modes 2-3) are tailored per role and grounded in the KB. - **Fixed** (mode 4) uses your chosen archetype as-is. ## 6. Reconcile (track replies) ```bash python3 tools/gmail_reconcile.py --apply # set INTERVIEW / REJECTED / SUBMITTED bash tools/reconcile_loop.sh # continuous, refreshes counts ``` ## 7. Adaptive fallback (opt-in) `ADAPTIVE=1` hands a `BLOCKED` task to `tools/adaptive/run.sh`, a separate agent on its own browser port and profile. It handles unknown forms and widgets; it stops on CAPTCHA, 2FA, rate limits, paywalls, fees, payment or ID uploads, and site terms. A verified confirmation is recorded as `SUBMITTED`; a wall stays `BLOCKED`. ## Environment switches (summary) | Env | Effect | |---|---| | `PARALLEL=n` | number of concurrent applications | | `REVIEW=1` | generate + gate + record `PREPARED`, do **not** submit | | `LIGHT=1 FIXED_CV=` | one fixed CV for all roles, no per-role generation | | `PRIORITISE=0` | keep file order instead of most-senior-first | | `ELIGIBILITY_OVERRIDE=...` | one-run override of the eligibility rules | | `ENGAGEMENT=contract` | use contract/consulting CV+letter rules (rate allowed) | | `AGENT=claude` | the coding agent each task runs with: `opencode`, `claude` or any CLI that takes the prompt as its last argument (default: opencode if installed, else claude) | | `MODEL=...` | the agent model the runner launches (opencode defaults to DeepSeek Flash; other agents use their own default) | | `CLAUDE_PERMISSION_MODE`, `CLAUDE_ALLOWED_TOOLS`, `CLAUDE_ARGS` | Claude Code permissions and extra flags (see [AGENT-SETUP.md](AGENT-SETUP.md#running-the-queue-with-claude-code)) | | `CAMOUFOX_SERVER=...` | target a specific browser instance/ports | | `KEEP_BROWSERS=1` | leave the Camoufox servers this run started running; by default they are stopped when the run ends | | `ADAPTIVE=1` | hand a `BLOCKED` task to the separate adaptive harness (forms only, never security controls) | Each parallel worker gets its own Camoufox server and profile. The runner stops the servers it started when the pool finishes or is interrupted, so a batch does not leave a full headless browser behind per worker. A server that was already healthy is reused and left alone, and the persistent profiles stay on disk, so a sign-in survives the restart. Use `KEEP_BROWSERS=1` only when you want the same servers for the next run. The runner works on Linux and macOS. macOS lacks `flock`, `setsid` and `timeout`, so `tools/compat/` provides portable stand-ins that are used only where the real commands are missing. If the project venv (`.venv`, from `tools/install.sh`) exists, the runner uses it automatically. The same goes for `human_assist.sh`, which also takes `AGENT`.

# The scam detector **A warning system, not a verdict.** [The hard rule](#the-hard-rule) · [Threat model](#threat-model) · [Signals](#signals) · [Email checks](#email-checks) · [Where it runs](#where-it-runs) · [The bucket](#the-probably-scams-bucket) · [Overrides](#overrides-and-clearing) · [Limits](#limits-and-false-positives) · [Extending](#extending-the-rules) · [Tests](#tests)
Job hunting attracts fraud. The patterns are not subtle once you know them, and they all end the same way: you install something, pay something, or hand over identity, bank or crypto credentials. `tools/scam_check.py` is the single rule set. It runs on every saved advert and every scanned message, and it feeds the dashboard's **Probably scams** bucket. It never submits, never clicks and never downloads anything. ## The hard rule > **Never download or install software, join a chat-only interview, share a > wallet, seed phrase or private key, pay a fee, or move money during a > recruitment process.** A real employer interviews over its own video link and > never needs remote-access tools. "Install AnyDesk so we can help you with the interview" is how a remote-access session is used to drain a crypto wallet or a bank account. "Install our trading app" and "share your seed phrase" are the same scam with a different wrapper. ## Threat model | The scam | What the attacker wants | What it looks like | |---|---|---| | Remote-access interview | Control of your machine and browser session | "Install AnyDesk/TeamViewer/RustDesk before the call" | | Crypto drain | Your wallet, seed phrase or private key | "Install Trust Wallet", "validate your wallet", "claim your signing bonus" | | Advance fee | A payment from you | Training, certification, equipment, onboarding, visa or a background-check fee | | Equipment cheque | Your bank account and a reversed cheque | "We'll send a cheque; buy the kit and send the balance back" | | Money mule | Your bank account as a laundering hop | "Receive payments and forward them", "keep a commission" | | Reshipping | Your address to receive stolen goods | "Receive packages, repackage and forward them" | | Task scam | Your own money or crypto, "unlocked" by fake earnings | "Complete tasks", "deposit to unlock more work" | | Crypto salary | A crypto payment rail and your wallet | "Salary paid in USDT", "deposit crypto to start" | | Labour trafficking | Your passport and your freedom | A job abroad, travel/visa fees, "we hold your passport" | | Recovery scam | A second fee from an earlier victim | "We can recover your lost crypto for a fee" | | Chat-only interview | Untraceable contact | The whole process runs on Telegram/WhatsApp/Signal | | Credential phishing | Your email or ATS login | A lookalike domain, a shortened or IP link, an unexpected login page | ## Free-mail senders A lead that arrives from a free mailbox (gmail.com, outlook.com, ...) is a MEDIUM signal even when the message contains no advert. The scan reads the sender recorded in the saved lead brief, so `email_opportunities.py` and `prepare_role.py` flag it automatically, and `scam_check.py --backfill` rescans older saved descriptions. The grid shows a scam marker and the role's drawer explains the signal. ## Signals Each signal has a stable `key` (shown in the scan JSON and the dashboard), a level, and an action. employment scams (`ic3.gov`, `fbi.gov`). - **Europol**: *How to spot fake job adverts*, *Crackdown on money mule service providers*, and the crypto-investment-fraud guidance (`europol.europa.eu`). - **Scamwatch (Australia)**: *Jobs and employment scams* (`scamwatch.gov.au`). - **NAB / ANZ**: employment-scam red flags and money-mule guidance. These sources describe the patterns; the scanner is a local heuristic layer, not a substitute for verifying the employer. It cannot detect a deepfake interview, a hijacked real advert, or a fake domain when there is no known company domain to compare against: those need the human checks below. ## Email checks The mail scan looks at more than the body: - **From domain vs the apply domain.** A lookalike is MEDIUM; a completely different domain is only a LOW note because agencies and job boards write from their own domains. Known ATS and job-board domains are never flagged. - **Reply-To.** A reply address that differs from the sender and is a free mailbox, an IP host or punycode is MEDIUM. - **Links.** Installers, raw IP hosts, punycode hosts, wallet-connect/claim URLs and file hosts carrying an executable or archive. - **Attachments.** Executables, installers, scripts and remote-access tools are HIGH; compressed archives are MEDIUM. - **Body and subject.** The signals in the table above. ## Where it runs | Step | Tool | Result | |---|---|---| | Job-ad ingest | `jd_guard.py`, `discover.py --fetch-jd` | `state/scam/.json` | | Document preparation | `prepare_role.py` | **Refuses a HIGH signal** (`PREP FAIL`, exit 3) | | Mail sync | `gmail_readonly.py --sync` | Prints `SCAM ` per message | | Mail reconcile | `gmail_reconcile.py` | Prints a **scam warnings** section, adds `scam` to the review item, and writes the worst warning per role to `state/scam-emails.json` | | Dashboard | `dashboard.py`, `tools/web/app.js` | scam marker on the grid, a red/amber banner in the drawer and the Gmail review, and the **Probably scams** bucket | The dashboard reads the advert scan and `state/scam-emails.json` and keeps the **worst** level per role, so the grid, the drawer and the bucket agree. ## The Probably scams bucket The bucket is deliberately conservative. A role enters it when: - the advert or a message has a **HIGH** signal; - or a **specific MEDIUM** signal: `lookalike-domain`, `reply-to-mismatch`, `punycode-link` or `archive-attachment`; - or **two independent MEDIUM** signals. A single free mailbox, a generic domain mismatch or an agency's own domain is only a note, not a bucket entry. That is intentional: agencies and ATS footers would otherwise fill the bucket and hide the real risk. The bucket sits beside **Active / Focus / Needs you**, and the **SCAMS** node in the Application states graph jumps straight to it. ## Overrides and clearing - **Preparation override:** `prepare_role.py --allow-scam` continues despite a HIGH signal. Use it only after verifying the employer yourself; the scan file stays on the record. - **Clear a warning:** the role drawer has **Clear scam warning** (with a confirmation). It removes the advert scan and the role's entry in `state/scam-emails.json`. Only use it after verifying the employer. - **Do not delete a warning to make a role look clean.** The warning is the point. ## Limits and false positives - The scanner is a **warning system, not a verdict**. A small employer can write from a Gmail address; a security advert can say "cryptography"; a legitimate ATS footer can contain a shortened link. These are notes, not gates. - A legitimate advert's own anti-fraud notice ("scammers may ask for payment for equipment") is recognised and skipped. - Email matching still decides which role a message belongs to. A marketing mail that matches a role can raise a warning there; verify before acting. - A HIGH signal is a gate because the cost of being wrong is asymmetric: one remote-access session can empty a wallet. ## Extending the rules Signals live in `SIGNALS` in `tools/scam_check.py`: ```python { "key": "remote-access-software", "level": "high", "re": r"...", "why": "why this is a scam pattern", "advice": "what the human should do", } ``` Add a specific regex, a level and the advice. Add a test in `tests/test_scam_check.py` for a positive and a negative case, and keep the patterns tight: a single ordinary word is not a signal. ## Tests ```bash python3 tools/scam_check.py --jd state/job-descriptions/.md python3 tools/scam_check.py --text "Download AnyDesk before the interview" --json python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_scam_check.py ``` The suite covers the high signals, the email/domain/link/attachment checks, the lookalike and real-domain cases, and the advert's own anti-fraud notice.
